The wedge is doing their FB sighting-coordination function properly (map-first, structured, trajectory-aware). Lead with the partnership, not scraping. See docs/decisions/007-community-uptake-strategy.md and docs/strategy/community-uptake.md.

title: Species pages: a profile page per cetacean species, linked from the whales page
description:
Peter, 2026-10-07: another agent is working on species pages; this issue holds what the whales page (decision 069, #633) leaves for it.

- /whales is prerendered by scripts/read-path/whales.ts using templates in src/whales.ts. Each species entry carries its register entity_id. Its <h2> heading and small map aren't links yet; point them at the new pages.
- Which reports are a species': cetaceans are register species whose register.taxon_ancestor lineage reaches Cetacea (SSA:0000934). An ecotype's reports reach its species through register.ancestor. The SQL is readInputs() in whales.ts, and the build now loads register.taxon_ancestor.
- Memory: a task that reads build.occurrences must be measured against production-sized documents (64,000 at about 1.1 KB). whales-page ran out of memory at 64 MB and froze manifest.json for 46 minutes (#634); it runs at 128 MB now. A failing export task blocks the manifest for the whole site.
- Small maps: src/small-multiples.ts renderSmallMap(dots, subject). Circles and tiles must close explicitly, because Lit's SSR parses SVG as HTML and nests self-closing ones until the stack overflows.
- Decision 069 rejects species pages 'for now'; amend it when they land. The nav (src/site-nav.ts) comes with renderProfileFrame(content, current).
- Read decision 070 (branch decision-070-srkw-generated, unmerged): pages follow populations, not register ranks (Bigg's, Southern Resident community and someday Northern Residents as peer pages, with pods the one extra level). That bears on how a species page lists its ecotypes and populations.
notes: Filed on a misunderstanding (2026-10-07): nobody is working on species pages. Peter chose not to build them yet (decision 069). Deferred, not closed, so the notes are here when someone does.

title: Smoke fails on any deploy before the day's first sighting: today's day file 404s by design
description: A day with no occurrences has no day file (scripts/read-path/occurrence-days.ts, since salish-t3g.1), and the client treats the 404 as an empty day (src/read-path.ts). But Chromium logs 'Failed to load resource: 404' as a console error, and e2e/smoke.spec.ts requires zero console errors, so any deploy between Pacific midnight and the first sighting of the day goes red with production fine. Seen on run 37655571859 (02a5cb0, 2026-10-07 10:08 PT; GH #636). Fix options: point the smoke at a date with sightings (?d=yesterday or a fixed past date), ignore exactly that day-file 404 in the console check, or have the build write an empty [] for every day through covered_through so the 404 never happens (also removes a 404 every visitor sees on a quiet morning).

title: The ingest heartbeat runs every 4–6 hours, not every 30 minutes, so a stall shorter than that is never reported
description: On 2026-10-06/07 the whales page (#633) failed every build for 46 minutes (00:11–00:57Z) and froze manifest.json. heartbeat.ts's 'unpublished' check (PUBLISHED_MINUTES 30) would have filed an issue, but ingest-heartbeat.yml's */30 schedule ran only at 00:34, 07:09, 14:21, 19:40 and 23:32 UTC on 10-06: GitHub's cron lateness is now hours, not the median 68 minutes measured in August. Decision 012's latency premise ('roughly 30–60 minutes') no longer holds. Options, none chosen: (a) Sentry Crons: fly/build.sh checks in after the manifest is written; Sentry alerts on a missed check-in. 012 rejected this for a second channel and new dependency, but Sentry is now in use (frontend, deploy source maps). (b) An external uptime checker on /read-path/manifest.json's age. (c) Trigger the heartbeat by workflow_dispatch from somewhere reliable. Amend or supersede 012 with whatever is chosen.
close_reason: PR #635 (5cf822b): fly/build.sh checks in to Sentry cron monitor read-path-build (ok when manifest.json rewritten, error otherwise, missed when no build); 6 consecutive → issue. Decision 012 amended; runbook section. Alert connection in Sentry left to Peter (MCP token lacks alerts:write).

title: A Whales page lists the cetacean species we hold reports of, linked from a site nav (About · Map · Whales)
description: Peter, 2026-10-06: a whales page linked from the nav, listing species. Chosen: cetaceans only (register taxa under Cetacea, SSA:0000934 / NCBITaxon:9721, read from register.taxon_ancestor); each species shows common and scientific name, report count, last reported, and a small map (decision 067's static maps); killer whale lists its ecotypes, linking to the pages that exist (Bigg's); no per-species pages yet; the nav goes on every page: the map's header (replacing the info link), About, the profile pages (replacing 'Back to the map') and the whales page. Prerendered by the read-path build at /whales.
close_reason: PR #633 (e3a4862): /whales lists 18 cetacean species with counts, last report and small maps; killer whale links Bigg's; About · Map · Whales nav on every page; register.taxon_ancestor loaded; Stelis 530712c whales-page task; decision 069.

title: Map jumps sideways about a second after load
description: On first load without x/y/z, the map drew the hardcoded default view and then, once every tile had loaded (rendercomplete), fit to the region — a ~190 km sideways jump plus a zoom change. Fit on the first change:size with area instead.
close_reason: Merged in #630

title: A deploy run stuck 'waiting' on the production environment jams every later deploy; give the Deploy job a timeout or let the concurrency group cancel in progress
description: Twice on 2026-10-06 a deploy.yml run's Deploy job sat 'waiting' on the production environment for hours with nothing to wait for: the environment's only protection rule is a branch policy, no reviewers, no wait timer, and pending_deployments reported no reviewers and current_user_can_approve=false — GitHub had lost the deployment. e532003's run from 15:12Z (the other agent cancelled it) and 105e121's from 19:06Z (cancelled 22:1xZ). Because deploy.yml's concurrency group deploy-production has cancel-in-progress: false, every later run queued behind the stuck one and GitHub kept only the newest pending (600217f and others were cancelled as superseded), so main was not deploying for three hours each time and nothing reported it. Options: a timeout-minutes on the Deploy job (a legitimate deploy takes ~10 min; 'waiting' for 30 is a stall), or cancel-in-progress: true on the group (the newest main always wins, which is already the workflow's stated rule for superseded commits), or both; and a way to see the stall — the heartbeat or a scheduled check that main's head has deployed. Owner of the deploy rework (salish-t3g.5/.9) to decide.
close_reason: PR #627 (d203765): a Watch job in deploy.yml cancels a run whose production deployment GitHub lost, after 15 min without a runner, files deploy-failed, and dispatches one fresh run of main. Decision 024 amended; runbook gotcha 4. Scheduled workflows: salish-7tkc.

title: Design: show several bouts in one day at one hydrophone
description:
Peter, 2026-10-06: open design problem. How should the map show several bouts heard at the same hydrophone on the same day?

Prod, 2026-10-06 (public.acoustic_bouts; days in Pacific time): 163 bouts over 133 hydrophone-days. 25 of those days (19%) have 2-4 bouts. 100 orcasound occurrences are on the map.

Worked example, 29 Jan 2026:
- Orcasound Lab had 4 bouts: 15:19-15:22, 15:45-16:10, 21:32-21:36, 21:33-21:37.
- Andrews Bay had 3: 15:19-15:22, 16:42-16:44, 21:33-21:37.

Why it's hard:
- Every bout at a feed sits on the hydrophone's exact coordinate, so the markers stack perfectly. The occurrence layer's declutter (decision 029) then hides all labels but one.
- Decision 053 splits a bout into one occurrence per species, which adds more stacked markers at the same point.
- Same-feed bouts overlap, e.g. 21:32-21:36 and 21:33-21:37. They look like two moderators bouting one event. Ask orcasite/Scott whether these are duplicates.
- Neighbouring hydrophones hear one event at the same time (Orcasound Lab and Andrews Bay, 15:19-15:22 and 21:33-21:37). So is it one acoustic event or two?
- A bout has a duration, which a sighting doesn't (salish-8vr.25 gave occurrences an end time). A point marker has nowhere to show it.

Options, none chosen:
(a) One marker per hydrophone per day, with a 24-hour ring around the hydrophone icon. Each bout is an arc for its time span, in the species colour, with a minimum arc width so a 3-minute bout stays visible. The label carries the count and the identifiers. The card lists the bouts in time order. One glyph shows how many bouts, when, and for how long.
(b) Same aggregation, but a count badge instead of the ring. Simpler, but it hides time of day.
(c) Keep one marker per bout and spread them out on click. Smallest change, but the map still shows one marker until someone clicks it.
(d) For display only, merge overlapping or near-adjacent bouts at a feed into one listening episode. This fixes the duplicate-looking pairs, not the separate morning and evening bouts, so it would complement (a) or (b), not replace them.

Also open: whether simultaneous bouts at neighbouring hydrophones belong in one segment (decision 063 joins by space and time), which would give the map a single acoustic track.

title: Ask for Finwave partner-API access to the Bigg's catalogue
description:
Peter, 2026-10-06: Jared Towers, who maintains the West Coast Transient catalogue (formerly with DFO, now Bay Cetology), is behind finwave.io, and an integration looks easy to get.

Why: the community Bigg's sheet we import (BIGGS-SHEET, salishsea-io data/biggs-ids.tsv) is stale. The live export on 2026-10-06 is byte-identical to our 2026-07-07 mirror, Google shows it last modified 2025-07-01, it lists 5 calves from 2025 and none from 2026, and it lacks T419-T421, which Bay Cetology designated in March 2026. Bay Cetology assigns the T designations, so Finwave is the authority the sheet copies. This is the likely answer to animals Q3 (animals#3): Finwave for designations and families, the sheet only for nicknames and their origins.

What Finwave offers (docs.finwave.io, read 2026-10-06). This replaces animals sources.tsv's 'no documented API (checked 2026-08-13)':
- A 'V1 partner API at /api/v1/...', described as read-only access to a population's data. It is mentioned in web/administration/datasets-api; no reference page for it is published. It isn't called from the web bundle, so it presumably needs a key.
- Individuals carry an identifier, alternative IDs (other catalogues' designations, e.g. the Alaska AM numbers in Q23), sex, birth/death years and relationships.
- Licence and visibility are set per organisation. No public population pages answer at srkw/biggs/wct.finwave.io.

To do: (1) Ask Scott whether he'll introduce us, or contact Jared directly. Ask for partner-API access to the Bigg's population, its terms, and the licence of what we may republish (designations and genealogy are facts; check the rest). (2) Once access is granted: a register ADR in salish-sea/animals, like ADR-0023 for NOAA's Southern Residents, plus a rights entry. (3) Correct the FINWAVE/BAYCETOLOGY notes in animals data/sources.tsv.

title: derive-occurrences, candidates and profile links recompute only the source arms whose inputs changed (STELIS_CHANGED_INPUTS)
description: occurrences.sql already writes one INSERT per source with a source column. Given STELIS_CHANGED_INPUTS (newline-separated artifact names; absent = recompute whole), map each arm to the inputs it reads, DELETE that arm's rows and re-INSERT it; skip the TS helpers (maplify entities, inaturalist scope) the untouched arms need. Same for identifier-candidates (per occurrence source) and profile-links. Verify: a save build's derive-occurrences from 5.6 s to well under 1 s; outputs byte-identical to a full recompute (compare after the next scheduled full build, which must still cut off).
notes:
PR #621 (branch derive-by-source). Verified on a copy of the live snapshot + mirrors (taken under the lock 2026-10-06 evening): full run, native-only partial (STELIS_CHANGED_INPUTS=public.observations) and maplify+inaturalist partial all reproduce the digest of the table the Fly build wrote (66,037 rows); native-only under 1 s on the laptop vs 2 s full (Fly: 5.6 s full → expect ~0.5 s). Four local reviews (CodeRabbit capped) found: view binding order (memory tables before the views), one-writable-db-per-transaction, and all-arms-in-one-transaction memory shape — all fixed. Scheduled builds still rebuild every arm (inaturalist_mirror.taxa restamps checked_at each run; it is shared by design). Pin: fly/stelis-commit = 339a4619338a92c14ef3fb197b7aab78a4369716. Possible follow-up: exclude checked_at from taxa's observed columns on the Stelis side so ingest builds can go partial too.
Merged #621 (81db289), deployed by the workflow as Fly v87 with Stelis 339a461. On the machine, under the lock: STELIS_CHANGED_INPUTS=public.observations → 'build.occurrences: 66042 rows (native re-derived; the rest as they were)', 1.15 s wall including node start, against 5.6 s running + 0.8 s observing for the full derivation in a build.
close_reason: Live on Fly v87: a save re-derives the native arm alone, ~1 s instead of ~6.4 s; outputs digest-identical to the full derivation.

title: A save's build does one sighting's work: recompute by source, rebuild files per day (Stelis ADR 0015)
description: The save-triggered build (salish-9uu.6, 13 tasks, ~20 s) re-derives all ~64,000 occurrences and rewrites every day file, id shard and calendar month for one row. Step 1: the three derivations read STELIS_CHANGED_INPUTS and recompute only the source arms whose inputs changed (a save: the native arm), replacing those rows in build.*. Step 2: once Stelis observes build.occurrences per Pacific day, occurrence-days/ids/calendar honour STELIS_REBUILD_KEYS and write only the moved keys.

title: A sighting saved here is shareable at once: a public by-id read, and the page, card and preview fall back to it
description: A visitor saves a sighting and shares the link. Until the build lands (about a minute; up to a few) the ?o= link finds nothing in the id shard, the card renderer 404s and caches the miss for five minutes, and the OG handler's text falls back to Supabase, where no save has landed since the cutover. Fix: GET /api/sightings/<id> for anyone, answering the sighting as the build would publish it (the page's ownOccurrence approximation, species names from the export dir's animal-names.json); the page's ?o= lookup, the card renderer and the OG edge handler fall back to it when the files have no such id (replacing their dead Supabase arms). The build stays the one publisher; this only bridges the minute before it.

title: The Stelis pin lives in the repo, so a workflow can build the image
description: fly/deploy.sh takes STELIS_SHA from the operator's environment; nothing in the repo says which Stelis commit production runs, so a workflow can't build the image. Commit the pin (a file under fly/ or the Dockerfile's ARG default) and have deploy.sh read it. A Stelis bump then becomes a reviewed PR here and ships atomically with the site (the reason beeatlas ADR 0042 pins Stelis into the image). Find the currently deployed SHA first (the running image's /opt/stelis, or the last deploy's args).
notes: Production runs Stelis 9e34f58bfa6e7d6b4055168597e8529d3b22b317 (Peter, 2026-10-06; deployed with e532003 and 5ea113a). Image tags since decision 066 name it too: registry.fly.io/salishsea-io:<sha>-stelis-9e34f58bfa6e.

title: The Fly machine shuts down cleanly: a deploy waits for the running build and stops Litestream before the machine goes
description: fly/start.sh trapped no signal and fly.toml set neither kill_signal nor kill_timeout, so every deploy ended Caddy, the running build, the write API and Litestream at Fly's SIGKILL (bash's background jobs ignore the default SIGINT). Decision 066: fly/deploy.sh builds and pushes the image, then takes /data/build.lock over fly ssh (waiting out a running build) before deploying it; on SIGTERM start.sh stops the schedule, the write API (Litestream forwards; the API finishes in-flight requests) and lets Litestream make its final sync, then Caddy, without waiting for builds — Fly has already stopped routing to the machine, so waiting there would be downtime.
close_reason: Verified on production 2026-10-06 (second deploy of 5ea113a): SIGTERM → litestream forwards → api: stopping → litestream shut down → Caddy → main child exited 0, ~1 s. #609 + #610 (kill_signal had been filed under [build]).

title: Infra: photo bucket served at /media/, replica bucket, scoped credentials (CDK, 065)
description: CDK in infra/: a public-read photo bucket (or prefix) behind a CloudFront /media/* behavior on salishsea.io's distribution; a private Litestream replica bucket beside BackupBucket; an IAM user or role whose credentials write only those two prefixes, for the Fly machine's secrets. Lands through the deploy workflow's cdk deploy.
notes:
2026-10-05: also a CloudFront behavior for /api/* on salishsea.io's distribution: all methods (POST/DELETE), forward Cookie and Origin, no caching (CachingDisabled + an origin request policy with cookies and the Origin header). The default behavior is set up for a static site and would strip both.
From the Fable review of sign-in: the default behavior is Managed-CachingOptimized with GET/HEAD only and no origin request policy, so /api/* through salishsea.io would be refused (POST/DELETE 403 at the edge), lose Cookie and Origin, and could cache one user's /api/me for another at min TTL. The /api/* behavior needs CachingDisabled, an origin request policy forwarding cookies and the Origin header (AllViewer, or one naming them), and ALLOW_ALL methods.
And an origin custom header on the Fly origin, x-origin-verify: <secret>, the same secret set as the Fly app's EDGE_SECRET: the API believes CloudFront-Viewer-Address (the feedback rate limit's key) only on requests carrying it, since the Fly app is reachable directly. Forward CloudFront-Viewer-Address to the origin in the /api/* behavior's origin request policy.

Buckets salishsea-io-media + salishsea-io-store-replica (names checked free), IAM user salishsea-io-store-writer (PutObject media/*; List/Get/Put/Delete store/*), /api/* and /media/* behaviors placed after /cards/* so the renderer's origin id holds. cdk diff vs live: additions only. title: Postgres's inaturalist.taxa is still a derivation input, kept fresh by taxa-refresh.yml
description: After step C, 'Postgres holds only what users write' will not be true: derive/sources.sql:439-446 unions the iNaturalist mirror's taxa with every Postgres row the mirror lacks (~395), and taxa / species_id, inaturalist_taxon_name, the pinniped walk (haulout-nearby.sql:19-24) and the DwC classification all read that union. What keeps Postgres's copy alive now is not pg_cron (unscheduled in #560) but the weekly taxa-refresh.yml, which writes production through the pooler DSN every Monday. The sources.sql comment ('until the register's taxa are fetched in the build too') has no bead. Two concrete failures: a new register mapping to a taxon in neither set gives every Maplify, native and Happywhale occurrence for that animal species_id: null and the fallback scientific name, silently; and a retired taxon present in the mirror shadows a Postgres row that knows its current_taxon_id (mirror wins, sources.sql:438; cf. salish-c4c). Decide: fetch the register's taxa closure in the build (the mirror's taxa table gains what taxa-refresh fetches), or list this as a 059 step-4 item and say so in 061. Found in the 2026-10-04 review of salish-xv35.

title: The Maplify name guard's baseline is undeclared forward-only state with no curator override, and its hold stops every source
description: Three problems with maplify-names.json (check-maplify-names.ts:14-27, 88-96), each of which Postgres's Maplify ingest is currently covering for and which will bite once that ingest is unscheduled (step C). (1) It is the only state the build owns that cannot be regenerated — once the Postgres bootstrap (postgresAnswer, :103) goes, a lost volume means the guard passes vacuously — yet it is declared nowhere in salishsea.rkt (the gate's only declared output is the maplify-names-hold token, :414-421), is not replicated (no Litestream, nothing in fly.toml), and has no --history timeline. Under Stelis ADR 0013 it is 'authoritative'; declare it so. (Stelis note: cache.rkt:459-462's comment says an authoritative output cannot have a producer, contradicting model.rkt:357 — filed in the stelis repo; resolve before declaring.) (2) There is no acknowledgement path. A curator who deliberately removes a mis-mapped name from the register fails every build 'until the register names it again'; deleting the file by hand falls back to Postgres's stored entity_id, which holds the same pair. Postgres's resolve-maplify.ts refusal had the same shape but blocked one curator script. Proposal: a curator-editable allow-list artifact (an input to the gate, so the hold clears on a declared change). (3) maplify-names-hold is an input of derive-occurrences and dwca (salishsea.rkt:201-205), so a Maplify-only problem stops iNaturalist and Orcasound sightings reaching the map too. Either state that as the chosen trade in 061 or narrow the hold to the Maplify arm. Found in the 2026-10-04 review of salish-xv35.
acceptance_criteria: maplify-names.json is a declared artifact with provenance 'authoritative', replicated off the machine; a documented curator action clears a legitimate un-naming without editing files on the volume; 061 records whether the hold is site-wide or Maplify-only.
notes:
PLAN 2026-10-04 (Peter's model: reject input that would leave us inconsistent, i.e. fail the register upgrade; the build-side gate is the backstop). Today register-refresh.yml commits the edition (load.ts --apply) and only then runs resolve-maplify.ts, whose refusal leaves Postgres's stored identifications alone while the register is already upgraded; the build cannot do that half-measure, so the rejection moves BEFORE the load. (1) The build publishes its baseline at /status/maplify-names.json (Caddy, beside ingest-runs.json). (2) register-refresh.yml, before load.ts --apply: build the candidate edition's name index from the release TSVs (NAME_INDEX_SQL in DuckDB over the parsed tables, as the build does), resolve every pair in the published baseline, and refuse the load — workflow red, failure issue, Postgres untouched — if a pair that resolves today would resolve to nothing. resolve-maplify.ts keeps running after the load until Maplify's Postgres ingest is unscheduled, then retires. (3) The build's gate stays site-wide: it now fires only if something bypassed the workflow (a hand --emit-sql load), which is an inconsistent state and should stop every published file; say so in 061. (4) An intended un-naming is a change to a checked-in allow-list of (name, scientific name) pairs that BOTH checks read: the workflow to permit the load, the gate to drop the pair from its baseline. Declared as an input of the gate, so the change clears the hold through a declared input moving. Replication of maplify-names.json: Fly volume snapshots (daily) plus the published copy; nothing more until it has a Litestream home with the mirrors.
2026-10-04 (CodeRabbit on #568, taken): while resolve-maplify.ts still runs after load.ts in register-refresh.yml, it must read the same allow-list and exempt listed pairs from its loss refusal — otherwise an accepted un-naming loads the edition and then fails the workflow, the half-measure the plan is meant to remove.
2026-10-04 (Fable): DONE, #569 (9d93209) + Stelis e043432, live on Fly v54. (1) /status/maplify-names.json published (no-cache). (2) register-refresh.yml refuses an edition before load.ts via scripts/register/check-unnaming.ts (edition read as the build reads one; the gate's own judge). Verified locally against the real latest edition 2026.09.6 and the live baseline: passes; with a pair no edition names added, refused exit 1 naming it; with that pair allow-listed, passes. Not run as a workflow against production (that loads the register; Peter's call) — the next register release, or a manual gh workflow run, is its first real run. (3) data/maplify-unnamed.tsv is the allow-list, read by the check, by resolve-maplify.ts (--allow) and by the build's gate as a declared authoritative input. (4) Hold stays site-wide as the backstop; 061 and 049 amended. Replication of the baseline: Fly volume snapshots + the published copy; a Litestream home with the mirrors is still open.

title: A source outage is recorded as 'unchanged' in the build's own history
description: If iNaturalist is down for a day, every build's trace, --explain --last and the operator build log say 'iNaturalist: source unchanged — ingestion skipped' for the whole outage; only /status/ingest-runs.json knows the fetch failed. Decision 061's consequence — the heartbeat's 'is the source reachable' question moves to Stelis's build history and operator log — is therefore not met. Cause: ingest-orcasound.ts:142-144 (same shape in ingest-maplify.ts:179-182 and ingest-inaturalist.ts:309-310) computes records = run.ok ? run.changed : 0 and writes the STELIS_BOUNDARY_RECEIPT as {unchanged: true, records: 0}, and the receipt shape (Stelis exec.rkt read-boundary-receipt, st-8bj) has no failure arm, so exec.rkt:477-484 prints and records 'unchanged'. Fix: the Stelis side adds a failure arm to the receipt (filed in the stelis repo under st-ml9 as 'a boundary receipt can say the source was unreachable'); then each ingest script writes it on !run.ok. Keep 'the mirror keeps its last good copy and the build goes on' (#559) — only the record changes. Found in the 2026-10-04 review of salish-xv35 (Stelis-side finding and salishsea-side finding independently).
acceptance_criteria: A build whose fetch failed shows a distinct line in run-plan's output, in --explain --last and in the operator build log, and the trace record carries the error text; ingest-runs.json is unchanged.
close_reason: Stelis 9074359 + #565 (deployed Fly v52): a failed fetch writes {unreachable, error}; the trace, --explain --last and the operator log say 'source unreachable — kept the last good copy'.

title: A 10-day window misses Maplify sightings published or revised late: decide how far back the build re-fetches
description: Found 2026-10-02 backfilling the build's Maplify mirror over 2014-04..2026-10 (150 month windows) and comparing it with Postgres's store over the whole history. Every difference is Postgres not having re-fetched past its 10-day window: (a) 66 in-scope sightings Postgres never got, Oct 2025-May 2026, e.g. maplify:237787, a harbor porpoise dated 2025-10-11 — Maplify published them after their date had left the window; (b) 62 Postgres still shows that Maplify now reports under an excluded source (rwsas/wras), some at another place and name, e.g. 238926; (c) 19 timestamps Maplify trimmed to the minute and 1 edited comment; (d) 1,160 comments Postgres holds as '' that the core now normalizes to null (rows stored before blankToNull). The build's ingest has the same window, so it will miss late arrivals the same way. Options (Peter's call): a periodic wider re-fetch (e.g. nightly 90 days, or the whole history weekly: 150 requests, ~1 min, ~17 MB mirror), or widen the per-build window. At cutover (.9) the map changes accordingly: +66, -62 sightings, and ~1,200 day-file documents change (body '' -> null, 19 times).
close_reason: Peter, 2026-10-02: widen to 30 days and add anti-entropy. #547 (6465d96) + Stelis 04de3a3, deployed to Fly 2026-10-03 01:03Z. Each build fetches the 30 days ending today plus one older calendar month sampled with BeeAtlas's recency weighting (1/(1+age in years)), each reconciled whole. Live: '2026-09-03..2026-10-03: 1129 fetched; unchanged' then '2020-12-01..2020-12-31: 53 fetched; unchanged'. Postgres's ingest keeps 10 days until the cutover.

title: Port the profile pages' link views to the build, gated like the occurrences

They derive from derived.occurrences, the identifier candidates, and for bouts public.acoustic_identifications (register.taxon_entity_for over bout entities). Until they are derived in the build, no source's Postgres ingest can stop without freezing profile pages on what Postgres last saw. Port them as DuckDB twins over build.occurrences, build.occurrence_identifier_candidates and the mirrors (decision 061's pattern: twin each view and the functions it calls, write the same documents to_jsonb does, gate against the snapshot's copies), then switch the four page tasks' inputs. title: Profile pages read the snapshot's year, not snapshot-meta, so a no-op build skips them

title: Resolve Maplify's entity and collection in the derivation, not at ingest
description: Decision 061 and Peter's rule that a mirror holds only what upstream said: maplify.sightings' entity_id and collection_id are resolved by the ingest today (scripts/ingest/maplify.ts resolveEntity against the register name index; maplify.resolve_collection's rule table). The DuckDB port (xv35.2) still reads both resolved columns from the snapshot. Port the resolution into the derivation: entity via the name index (fetchNameIndex's query over register.entities/names/ancestor/deprecations, already in the snapshot, plus src/fold.ts and scripts/register/name-index.ts), collection via maplify.collection_rule (snapshotted; note resolve_collection's UNION ALL ... LIMIT 1 relies on branch order for precedence, which Postgres doesn't strictly guarantee — make the precedence explicit in the twin). Prerequisite of the Maplify ingest moving (xv35.7), whose mirror won't carry those columns.

title: Prototype identity-first travel segments
description: Build segments with named identities (occurrence_identifications: status, certainty, evidence) as the spine and position-only joining as the fallback, plus a first guess at per-sighting position radii by source (hydrophone, shore report, GPS). Compare against the current rule and the nearest-point / space-time / ecotype-check variants on 2026-09-03 (Scott's day, Admiralty Inlet) and 2023-06-24 (T36s/T65As zigzag). Must not assume matrilines travel together: groups join and split, individuals wander. title: Cutover: downstream reads the ported occurrences, pg_cron's ingest is unscheduled per source, the Deno function retires
description: Decision 061, the end of step 3. Preconditions: xv35.2/3 gates green long enough, xv35.4 overlay live, xv35.5 cadence decided and deployed, each source's mirror gate green. Then: occurrence-days/calendar/ids/profiles take occurrences_ported as input and the gate nodes are retired; one migration per source unschedules its pg_cron job and stops writing ingest.runs for it; the heartbeat's two questions move to Stelis's build history / operator build log; the Deno function, its trigger secret and the Vault entries go last. Afterwards Postgres holds native sightings, photos, feedback, the catalogue, the register load and sign-in — what step 4 (059) moves. The day files change bytes exactly once here (Postgres vs DuckDB rendering); say so in the PR.

In the build, resolution is live from the snapshot's register, so an edition that loses a name silently drops those Maplify sightings from the map (measured: renaming one register name dropped 30). title: Measure a five-minute build cadence on the Fly machine before the overlay cutover
description: Decision 061: the build's cadence becomes the ingest's (every 5 min today). Owed since st-ml9's first slice: on the Fly machine, what a build that finds nothing costs (wall time, peak RSS, DB reads), what one changed day costs, and how .stelis/ history grows at 288 builds/day (log lines, blocks, render-log size). Decide the crontab cadence from the numbers and whether the listener stays. Stelis-side counterpart filed under st-ml9.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-10-01 on Fly (production data, scratch dirs, build lock held, /proc sampled every 0.5 s):
- Cold build (every task runs): 96 s. Warm build (nothing changed): 68 s. Of the warm build: snapshot ~30 s (re-reads Postgres every build); Stelis relation digesting ~35 s (duckdb CLI launches, several per relation x ~40 relations, each opening the ~330 MB snapshot); the four profile-page tasks ~13 s, rerun every build because their snapshot-meta input changes every build though they use only its year; output identical.
- Real cadence: 330 builds 2026-09-28..10-01 (~95/day); occurrence-days reran in 150 of 330 (47 of the last 100): about half of builds see changed occurrences.
- Memory: lowest free 228 MB during occurrence-days (366 MB) — see xv35.10/#541. Racket ~130 MB resident through the build.
- History: /data/stelis 51 MB after 330 builds. Log line ~25 KB/build (was ~15 KB before #531's 25 relations). Blocks ~13.5 MB/day; 36 of 42 MB are 249 KB copies of days/'s per-file map, rewritten whole whenever any one day changes.
PROJECTION at a 5-minute cadence (288 builds/day, ~20-50% changing data): no-op build 68 s = ~23% of the single CPU; history ~7 MB/day of log + ~15-36 MB/day of day-map blocks = roughly 0.7-1.3 GB/month against 2.3 GB free on the volume. Not viable as-is.
WHAT WOULD MAKE IT VIABLE (filed): page tasks read a year relation instead of snapshot-meta (salishsea+Stelis, small: -13 s and the 260 MB individuals step on no-op builds); Stelis batches relation digests into one duckdb process (engine: -~30 s); Stelis chunks keyed maps so one changed day rewrites one small chunk, plus a history retention policy (engine). After ingest moves into the build, the snapshot no longer reads Postgres and the ~30 s goes too.

CPU, the binding constraint (found 2026-10-02 00:30Z): the same cold build that took 96 s at 23:40Z took 1,033 s at 00:19Z, every step 10-20x slower including untouched ones. /proc/stat over 5 s: user 6%, system 2%, STEAL 92%. Fly's shared-cpu-1x quota is 5 ms per 80 ms (6.25% of a core = ~1.5 CPU-hours/day), with unused time banked as burst credit up to 500 s, starting at 5 s on every machine start — so each deploy resets it, and the boot build plus the listener's resubscribe build spend it at once (https://docs.fly.io/machines/cpu-performance). The 23:40Z measurements ran on banked credit. Demand: a no-op build is ~1 CPU-minute, a cold one ~1.5; at today's ~95 builds/day that is ~1.6-2.4 CPU-hours/day, already above the 1.5 baseline, and a 5-minute cadence (288/day) needs ~5+ CPU-hours/day before the engine work in st-ml9.6/st-ml9.7 and xv35.12. While throttled, builds take ~15 min and the listener keeps the machine saturated, so it doesn't recover on its own; Caddy still serves (home 1.1 s, data files 0.2-0.3 s), so visitors see staler data, not errors.
2026-10-02 ~06:32Z (Opus), Fly shared-cpu-4x, salishsea main 2164f5a + Stelis 52b099b: a no-op build (3 ok, 15 cached) takes 34 s wall, min MemAvailable 344 MB, engine RSS peak 178 MB. Was 51 s before st-ml9.6 (batched relation digests) and xv35.12 (pages skip no-op builds); st-ml9.8 removed a 528 MB engine spike at the end of every build (the build log loaded every build's keyed maps). Remaining wall time is mostly the snapshot task's Postgres read.
DECIDED 2026-10-03 (Peter): five-minute cron at the cutover (not before: until then every build refetches Maplify and iNaturalist while pg_cron does too); the listener stays (it carries native sightings to logged-out visitors within a build); chunk keyed maps (Stelis st-ml9.7) before the cadence change rather than grow the volume or shorten retention. Numbers behind it, measured on Fly 2026-10-03 (shared-cpu-4x): a typical build 56 s wall, 23 CPU-s, min ~290 MB free; at 288/day ~1.8 CPU-h/day of a ~6 CPU-h baseline, iNat ~2,000 req/day of 10,000; history ~16 MB/day at ~100 builds/day -> ~48 MB/day at 288 -> ~1.4 GB at 30-day retention on a 2.9 GB volume (0.6 GB used), mostly days/'s ~250 KB per-file map rewritten whole.
2026-10-03: the chunking prerequisite landed (Stelis st-ml9.7, 3a84ea4; Fly runs cddb556): days/'s history writes drop ~19x, so 288 builds/day stays well inside the volume at 30-day retention. What remains for .5 is the crontab line itself, at the cutover.
close_reason: Five-minute cron live on Fly (1-59/5, #554, 2026-10-03). First builds: no-op ~30 s (5-7 ok, 13-15 cached); min MemAvailable 346 MB during a snapshot.

title: Signed-in contributors read the day files with a live overlay of native sightings
description: Decision 061: the overlay. When a user is signed in, fetchOccurrences reads the day file for everything upstream and asks PostgREST only for native sightings (provider_slug=direct or equivalent), merging by id with the live row winning; the calendar adds live native counts to the file's; a ?o= link to a sighting younger than a build keeps its Supabase lookup; the realtime broadcast becomes 'refetch the overlay'. Shippable behind VITE_READ_SOURCE=static independently of the data work. This is what lets pg_cron's ingest be unscheduled at cutover instead of running doubled until step 4. Consequence to state in the PR: a contributor sees upstream sightings within one build rather than one ingest tick — so xv35.5 (cadence) is a prerequisite of the CUTOVER, not of shipping this.

Known hazards: \m/\M word boundaries and the lookbehind in register.fold (RE2 lacks both); register.inaturalist_taxon's ancestor/deprecation union; rank enum ordering in inaturalist.species_id; DISTINCT ON; happywhale per-row AT TIME ZONE (test the DST rows). title: Move ingest into the read-path build (decision 056 step 3, toward 059's end state)
description:
Step 3 of decision 056, and the prerequisite for decision 059's end state. Today three sources (Maplify, iNaturalist, Orcasound) are ingested into Postgres by pg_cron calling the Deno edge function (supabase/functions/ingest, decision 011's pure-core/imperative-shell split). Happywhale is not: it has no scheduled ingest, no ingest.runs rows and no TypeScript replacement, only rows already stored in the happywhale schema and three in-database HTTP functions (salish-mzz). Whether step 3 adds a Happywhale importer or only snapshots those stored rows is undecided, and it decides whether any Happywhale ingest work belongs in this epic. Postgres derives the map from them: five per-source views (derived.maplify_occurrences, inaturalist_, happywhale_, native_, orcasound_) plus derived.identifier_candidates, kept in the stored table derived.occurrences by triggers (decision 055; views in supabase/migrations/20260928120000_occurrences_stored.sql, ~lines 41-300). The read-path build (Stelis: a data-pipeline build system Peter maintains, github.com/rainhead/stelis; the graph is src/salishsea.rkt there) currently snapshots that finished table from Postgres.

Step 3 moves both halves into the build: the ingest's pure transforms write snapshots (files the build reads) instead of Postgres rows, and the five views and the identifier candidates are ported to DuckDB. The port is checked row for row against the stored derived.occurrences until they agree, which implies running both side by side for a while. After this, Postgres holds only what users write (about 600 sightings, their photos, feedback) and sign-in, which is what decision 059's small SQLite store then replaces in step 4.

Nothing a visitor sees should change. The Fly app keeps serving the same files; the build just stops needing Postgres for anything but user writes.
design: DESIGN RECORDED as decision 061 (docs/decisions/061-ingest-and-derivation-move-into-the-build.md), 2026-09-30, Fable session. Summary: (1) derivation first, ingest second — widen the snapshot to the raw source + reference tables in the SAME transaction as derived.occurrences, port the five views + identifier_candidates to DuckDB writing the SAME doc shape to_jsonb produces (so nothing downstream changes), gated by a Stelis rule-check that diffs ported vs stored on parsed docs and fails the build; (2) ingest per source, Orcasound → Maplify → iNaturalist, as node boundary tasks writing per-source SQLite mirrors (node:sqlite, keyed by source id, normalized records, NO resolved columns — entity_id/collection_id resolution moves to the derivation; Peter's policy: no authoritative state in mirrors), each with a mirror-vs-Postgres gate while both ingests run, reporting via STELIS_BOUNDARY_RECEIPT; (3) signed-in contributors read the files with a live overlay of native sightings BEFORE pg_cron's ingest is unscheduled, which makes the build cadence (5 min) a prerequisite of cutover and forces st-ml9's owed measurements; (4) Happywhale is a frozen table — snapshot once, an upstream leaf, no ingest; (5) mirrors are 'derived' (rebuild = backfill run over past windows; Maplify serves history, iNat per 041), only user writes are authoritative; (6) register load, catalogue, native sightings, contributors stay in Postgres this step. Children xv35.1–.9 carry the phases; Stelis-side engine work filed under st-ml9 in the stelis repo. Previous handoff notes (2026-09-29/30, Opus) remain valid for environment/verification habits: 1 GB Fly machine no swap, measure peak RSS per task, stream don't materialize, plain node not tsx, one DuckDB instance per process, never share a DB with Orcasound, gloss Stelis at first mention, local Supabase is NOT currently the prod mirror (nearly empty on 2026-09-30).

title: Anyone with the publishable key can make every open salishsea.io tab refetch from the database at once
description:
The map's live updates ride a public Supabase Realtime channel, 'occurrences', whose occurrences_changed broadcast makes every open tab refetch the day from PostgREST (src/salish-sea.ts, the broadcast handler). A public channel accepts sends from any client holding the publishable key, which every browser has — confirmed 2026-09-28 against the local stack: a plain supabase-js client with only that key sent the event and a subscriber received it.

So a forged broadcast, repeated, puts every visitor's query on the database at the same moment: the load pattern behind the 2026-08-31/09-01 timeouts (salish-xfo), on demand. The tab's jitter spreads a burst over a few seconds but doesn't limit how often.

Options, none chosen: make the channel private (Realtime Authorization, RLS on realtime.messages) so only the database's own realtime.send can publish, and give browsers read access; or rate-limit the refetch in the tab; or, on the static read path (decision 056), stop listening in signed-out tabs at all, since they poll the read-path manifest instead. The Fly machine's change listener (salish-t3g.6, PR #507) has the same exposure and bounds it by spacing builds two minutes apart.

title: Build the read path when the data changes: the Fly machine listens for occurrences_changed and rebuilds after a burst
description: Decided with Peter 2026-09-28 (options 1+3). In static mode a signed-out visitor lost live updates: the realtime broadcast refetches a file that only changes hourly. The manifest (salish-t3g.4) lets tabs notice a new build; this makes builds happen when the data changes. A listener on the Fly machine subscribes to the same public occurrences_changed broadcast the browser does and runs build.sh a few seconds after a burst; changes arriving during a build trigger one more build after it, never a dropped one. The hourly cron stays as the backstop for a missed broadcast. Only works while Supabase Realtime sends the broadcast: after the database moves (step 4) the change signal has to come from the new write path.
notes:
2026-09-28: PR #507. Deployed to the Fly app from branch read-path-listener (Stelis e19e977); subscribed to production's channel, catch-up build backed off the boot build's lock and retried. Hourly backstop moved to :01.
2026-09-28: first real production change triggered a build end to end (listener heard occurrences_changed → snapshot changed → days and manifest rewritten). CodeRabbit on #507 found the broadcast is forgeable (confirmed locally); bounded by spacing listener builds >=2 min apart (<=30 reads/hour under a flood) and fixed busy-retry being brought forward. Durable fix (server-only signal) is Peter's call; the same forgery already hits production browsers: salish-59se.
Correction to the note above: the two-minute spacing caps LISTENER-triggered builds at 30 an hour; the hourly backstop adds one more, so at most 31 production reads an hour from builds, plus one per machine restart.
close_reason: Delivered in #507 (merged 8482fe0), deployed to the Fly app from main: the machine builds after bursts of occurrences_changed, spaced >=2 min apart since the broadcast is forgeable; hourly build at :01 as backstop. Verified with a real production change. Late review follow-ups in #508. The durable server-only signal is Peter's call (see salish-59se).

title: Read the map, calendar, catalogue and profile pages from static files instead of Supabase
description:
Step 1 of salish-t3g, the salishsea half. The Stelis half is st-ml9 in the stelis repo, which builds the files this reads: one file per Pacific day for the map, per-day-per-region counts for the calendar, whole-table catalogue files, and one occurrence-links file per individual, group, ecotype and haul-out.

The point is that a logged-out visitor's page loads stop depending on the database being up. Everything a signed-out visitor reads moves to the static files; nothing else changes in this step:
- Signed-in reads stay on Supabase (the user's own contributor record, their last sighting).
- All writes stay on Supabase (upsert_observation, delete, photo upload, submit_feedback).
- Share links (?o=<id>) keep their Supabase lookup. The static answer is undesigned; the address-bar URL must stay the shareable link.
- The realtime broadcast keeps driving refetches for now; step 2 replaces it with polling an uncached manifest.
- The link-preview edge function and the card renderer keep their Supabase reads.
acceptance_criteria:
- Against a local Stelis build, the map, calendar and all four profile page types render the same as they do from Supabase.
- The e2e suite passes.
- With Supabase unreachable, a signed-out visitor still gets the map, calendar and profile pages.
notes:
2026-09-27, how this ships (agreed with Peter): no long-lived branch. The static reader merges to main behind a build-time switch, VITE_READ_SOURCE=supabase|static, set the way VITE_SUPABASE_URL already is. Production keeps building with 'supabase', so every PR goes through the normal test and deploy gate without changing what visitors see; the cutover (step 2) and any rollback are the same one-line config change.
The prototype deploy builds that same main with 'static' and runs as a Fly app named salishsea-io — named for what it will become, not for 'static', because under the beeatlas ADR 0042 shape this one machine ends up hosting the file server, the Stelis build, the write API, auth and ingest. Until DNS points at it, it is the prototype at salishsea-io.fly.dev; at the step-2 cutover the same app becomes production. It is salishsea's first non-production environment (both deploy.yml jobs target environment: production today). Expected breakage there, acceptable for a read-path prototype: Google sign-in until the origin is added to the OAuth client's authorized JavaScript origins, and the CSP in the HTML shells needs the new origin.
2026-09-27: first slice (the map's day files) in PR #502 — scripts/read-path/, decision 056, day-boundary test. The frontend switch (VITE_READ_SOURCE) is not in it yet.
Deletion (asked by Peter 2026-09-27): the BUILD handles it — writeDays rewrites days/ whole, so a day that loses its last occurrence loses its file (tested). What is NOT handled yet is everything after the build, and it belongs to serving (step 2): (1) the copy to the served dir must delete too — an rsync without --delete or an object sync that never removes would keep serving the stale file; (2) a browser or CDN holding the old file keeps showing the deleted sighting until it revalidates, so day files need no-cache/revalidate headers or content-hashed names behind an uncached manifest; (3) the frontend must read a missing day file (404) as 'no sightings', which is only honest if something authoritative — the manifest or the calendar counts — says the build ran and the day is empty, not missing.
Also for step 2 (from PR #502's review): nothing serializes concurrent read-path builds. writeDays swaps days/ with two renames and assumes one writer; the scheduler that runs the build must hold a per-project lock, as beeatlas's nightly and note publishes share publish.lock.
2026-09-27: the frontend switch is PR #503 — a signed-out visitor's day on the map reads the day file under VITE_READ_SOURCE=static; signed-in contributors keep Supabase. Still on Supabase: calendar, profiles, share links, link previews.
2026-09-28: PR #503 merged (c05a009) and deployed; production still reads Supabase (VITE_READ_SOURCE unset). Remaining for this issue: calendar, catalogue and profile pages reading their files once st-ml9 builds them.
2026-09-28: the calendar's counts are PR #509 (one file per Pacific month, read by signed-out visitors, revalidated on each new build; Stelis 29560f2). Parity in a browser: every circle identical over 12 month×region views.
2026-09-28: share links (?o=) open from files via a sharded id index — PR #510 (Stelis c1a1938). Browser parity with Supabase mode on 3 links (busy day, outside every region, unknown id). Remaining on Supabase for signed-out visitors: catalogue lookups on sighting cards, profile pages.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-30. Every signed-out read on the Fly app comes from build files: map days, calendar, share links (?o=), all four profile kinds, designation redirects, and now the sighting cards' designation links (catalog-codes.json, #526). Acceptance: with every request to supabase.co blocked, the live Fly site renders the map (2025-07-19: 99 cards, 169 profile links, identical to Supabase reachable), calendar and profile pages; parity with Supabase mode checked per step (#509, #510, #513, #516, #517, #526). Remaining Supabase calls for a signed-out visitor are sign-in, the sighting form's species list and the change feed, none of which they use.

title: identifications.certainty, and a bout's cited entities become identification rows (decision 054)
description:
Implements docs/decisions/054-certainty-is-the-asserters-status-is-ours.md.

1. Enum public.identification_certainty (certain, probable, possible); nullable column identifications.certainty (null = nobody asked; never default to certain).
2. CHECK on identifications.confidence tying it to a machine method (cv today) so a human hedge is never stored as a number.
3. A new identification_evidence value for sound (enum is LOCKED against DROP, ADD is fine).
4. The ingest writes public.identifications rows for acoustic_bout_entities (method upstream_import, the sound evidence, subject resolved from the entity_id via individuals/social_groups entity_id, one row per tag application) in place of today's round trip: entity -> register label -> occurrences.identifiers -> fold -> occurrence_identifier_candidates as text_mention/text_extraction, which misstates evidence and method and has no place for a hedge. Needs the least-privilege ingest role granted on identifications.
5. Map label: a possible identifier renders with a trailing ? (Killer whale · J, K, L?); probable and certain plain. Check src/identifiers.ts detectPod/detectEcotype against the ? before shipping.
6. Archive terms (dormant while bouts are out of DwC): identificationQualifier ? for possible / cf. for probable on a species-level hedge; a sub-species hedge stays inside unvalidatedIdentifiers with its ?.
7. A species reached only through possible entities is a hedged occurrence; choose how the occurrences view exposes it.

Parts 1-4 need no upstream change. Certainty VALUES arrive only once orcasite exposes item_tags with certainty on the bouts include (orcasite#1014, #1051; salish-8vr.8).
notes: 2026-09-26: PR open — https://github.com/salish-sea/salishsea-io/pull/498 (branch certainty-through-the-views). Row of record is acoustic_bout_entities + acoustic_identifications view, not identifications rows; see 054's implemented note. Close on merge.
close_reason: Merged in #498 (main 8d2f5e0fba5acefb824012bc37cfa9eb95463390). Migrations 20260926120000 + 20260926120100; acoustic_identifications view; certainty on occurrences and the map label; ingest parses/reconciles per-entity certainty (null until orcasite exposes item_tags).

title: Ingest iNaturalist's Alive/Dead annotation; show dead animals as dead on the map
description:
iNaturalist observers and identifiers annotate an observation 'Alive or Dead' (controlled term 17: Alive 18, Dead 19, Cannot Be Determined 20). We ingest none of it: OBSERVATION_FIELDS in supabase/functions/ingest/fetch-inaturalist.ts requests no annotations, so a stranded or floating carcass reads on our map as a live sighting.

SCALE (rough, from the iNaturalist API on 2026-09-23 over a box around the Salish Sea, not our exact ingest scope): about 287 of 11,298 cetacean and 618 of 23,345 pinniped observations are annotated Dead.

WANTED:
- Ingest the annotation into the inaturalist mirror, as iNaturalist states it (decision 008: the mirror is what the API returns). An annotation carries votes; iNaturalist shows one whose vote score is not negative, and we should read it the same way rather than inventing a threshold.
- Carry it to public.occurrences as the occurrence's vitality (alive / dead / undetermined / not annotated).
- Mark dead animals on the map as dead: a distinct symbol, and dead occurrences kept out of track segments (a carcass is not part of a travelling group's path; src/segments.ts chains by species and time).
- DwC-A: Darwin Core has a 'vitality' term (alive / dead / mixedLot / uncertain / notAssessed) that fits exactly; worth publishing it, checked against docs/data-provenance.md.

UNDECIDED: whether other sources carry the same fact (Maplify/Whale Alert stranding reports, our own sighting form) and should feed the same column; what the dead symbol looks like (the PR needs a visual summary and legend per the repo's convention); whether a dead record should also be excluded from an individual's 'last seen'.

title: Integrate salmon run data on the site, with Zoe Liu (a la liu-zoe/orcasalmon)
description:
Show Chinook salmon run data alongside our killer whale sightings, the way Zoe Liu's Orca Salmon Dashboard does (https://github.com/liu-zoe/orcasalmon, live at https://salmonorca.fly.dev), and do it in collaboration with Zoe rather than as a parallel reimplementation.

WHAT HER DASHBOARD HAS: daily Chinook abundance at two counting sites -- the Albion test fishery on the lower Fraser (DFO, catch per unit effort, early April to mid-October) and Bonneville Dam on the Columbia (Columbia Basin Research DART adult passage counts) -- set against Southern Resident sightings from Acartia and The Whale Museum.

WHAT WE HAVE TODAY: only a static map layer of the two counting sites (src/assets/orcasalmon-counting-sites.geojson, glossary term 'Salmon counting site' in CONTEXT.md) that links out to her dashboard. No run data.

UNDECIDED -- to settle with Zoe and Peter before building:
- Where the data comes from: her pipeline/dataset, or DFO and DART directly.
- What the site shows: e.g. run timing against sightings on the map's date, a panel per counting site, or salmon context on SRKW profile pages.
- Whether it belongs in the DarwinCore export at all (salmon counts are not occurrences of our taxa).
- Rights: DFO and DART terms of reuse, checked against docs/rights-policy.md.
- How the work is shared: credit, which repo holds what, whether her dashboard keeps running.

First step: reach out to Zoe.

title: Read sex, birth years and life status from the register (decision 051)
description:
Decision 051: everything we can consume from the register, we do. The register holds sex (register.entities.sex, F/M/U), birth (register.entities.born, EDTF: '1998', '2020-09', '../1961' = born by 1961) and life status (dist/current_status.tsv, alive/dead/presumed_dead/unknown, with ADR-0006's recorded/effective precedence -- NOT yet loaded into register.*). public.individuals holds its own sex, born_earliest/born_latest and life_status.

Measured locally against 2026.09.6 on 2026-09-22: sex is on 311 register rows vs 310 of ours and agrees on all 309 where both are M/F; one animal is female here and U in the register, one null here and U there. Birth: register has 487, we have 415; comparing needs an EDTF interval parse (not done). Life status: not compared (file not loaded).

Work: load current_status.tsv; reconcile each field and report disagreements before switching (a disagreement is a question for the register, not a silent override); then read them from the register and drop our columns. Life status drives which group members a sighting reaches (decision 050), so a change there changes individual pages' sighting history.
notes: 2026-09-24: PR #494. Reconciled vs 2026.09.6: born 0 diffs; sex 1 (T109A3A F? -> U); status: 56 blank-in-sheet animals have no register status (Peter: blank could mean anything) -> unknown. Loader copies via public.refresh_individual_vitals() in its transaction; register.current_status loaded; verify fails on drift or unread birth shapes; seed/parser stop producing vitals. Group mention rule amended to 'not known dead' (050) so the 56 keep 2,125 links.
close_reason: Done in #494, deployed 2026-09-24. The register loader copies sex, birth years and life status onto public.individuals via public.refresh_individual_vitals() in every load's transaction; verify reported 0 differences after the post-deploy reload. Production now: 367 alive, 57 deceased, 7 presumed deceased, 79 unknown (the register's 23 plus the 56 blank-in-sheet animals); T109A3A sex unset. Group mentions reach members not known to be dead (decision 050 amended).

title: register.taxon_for and taxon_entity_for: pin search_path to '' (definer-rights with public ahead of pg_catalog)
description: Both are SECURITY DEFINER with search_path 'register, public, pg_catalog' / 'register, pg_catalog'. Listing public before pg_catalog lets an object created in public shadow a built-in or operator the body uses. register.inaturalist_taxon_for (migration 20260922040000) was written with search_path = '' after CodeRabbit flagged it on #482; do the same for taxon_for (and check taxon_entity_for, which omits public and is probably fine). Needs every relation in the body schema-qualified. 🤖
close_reason: PR #483 merged and deployed 2026-09-22; all three register definer functions have search_path='' in prod; guarded by supabase/definer-search-path.test.ts

title: Stop keying our own data on iNaturalist taxon ids; the register is the dictionary now
description:
Reframes what is left of salish-53t, after 53t.1 and 53t.2 shipped the read path.

THE EPIC'S TITLE OVERSTATES IT. Identity does not 'belong to iNaturalist' any more: 62,811 of 62,993 occurrences (99.71%) already carry a register entity. What is actually true is narrower and worse-shaped — we use iNaturalist as a DICTIONARY for data that is not iNaturalist's:

- scripts/ingest/maplify.ts:15 — Maplify arrives as scientific-name STRINGS and we LEFT JOIN inaturalist.taxa by name purely to turn a name into an integer. A non-iNat source routed through iNat identifiers.
- upsert_observation resolves the sighting form's name string to an iNat integer, so our own submissions are keyed on iNat.
- public.individuals.taxon_id: 510 rows, ONE distinct value (41521, the column DEFAULT, never varied), while all 510 already carry entity_id. Its only reader is TAXON_LABELS in src/individual-page.ts:18 — a two-entry hard-coded map of iNat id to name, with "Bigg's killer whale" hard-coded beside it. That string is exactly what the register holds for SSA:0000002. It is the same defect as SUBSPECIES_FORMS, which decision 033 forbids twice over (composing a name we can read; keying on an iNat id where 033 says 'keyed on SSA:, never on a name').

WHAT MUST STAY. inaturalist.observations.taxon_id and inaturalist.taxa.current_taxon_id are the mirror keying on upstream vocabulary, which decision 008 requires. Not a defect and not in scope. The epic's original inventory listed them beside the others, which conflates two different things.

BLOCKED ON UPSTREAM, filed as animals#40: 13 genus entities (Eumetopias, Lontra, Zalophus, Phoca, Orcinus, Megaptera, Enhydra, Delphinus, Mirounga, Callorhinus, Phocoena, Tursiops, Balaenoptera) would close 124 of the 182 unkeyed records. Each is a genus over a species the register already holds. The register already mints higher taxa (Cetacea, Otariidae, Phocidae, Pinnipedia, Lutrinae, Aves), so these are gaps rather than policy. The dictionary cannot be dropped while any record has no register identity, because the fallback must exist for every record or not at all.

ORDER ONCE UNBLOCKED: (1) delete TAXON_LABELS and the hard-coded Biggs string, read the name from the register, drop public.individuals.taxon_id — smallest, most visible, removes the last composed-name table in the repo; (2) key public.observations on entity_id, which also captures ecotype identity the iNat key cannot express (rectipinnus -> SSA:0000002 Bigg's, ater -> SSA:0000003 Resident); (3) Maplify ingest resolves names against the register instead of inaturalist.taxa.

NOT A REGISTER GAP: Delphinus delphis bairdii (3 records) fails because migration 20260828120000 deliberately exempts Delphinus from the subspecies roll-up, since Maplify carries long- and short-beaked common dolphins separately. Do not mint an entity for it.
notes: 2026-09-22, VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION after deploy of 6e7e3da. public.individuals.taxon_id no longer exists (0 columns); 510 individuals intact; public.animal_names holds 786 rows. SSA:0000002 -> "Bigg's killer whale", and an individual with no ecotype in its chain falls back to "Killer whale" -- both the strings the deleted TAXON_LABELS produced. An ANONYMOUS REST request against production returns HTTP 200 with the right row, so the REVOKE-then-GRANT is correct where it matters: a missing grant would have rendered every profile with no species line and raised nothing.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22. Our own sightings: #482 (decision 048). Maplify: #484 (decision 049) + #485 (ingest role grant). Register editions 2026.09.5 and 2026.09.6 added the names/taxa needed; in prod every identified Maplify record reaches a register entity (4,571 moved to Southern Resident SSA:0000010, 9 gained, 0 lost). No table of ours keys on an iNaturalist taxon id except the iNaturalist mirror itself (decision 008).

title: Cut dwc.taxa_classification over to the register's NCBI lineage, keeping kingdom=Animalia
description: Part 2 of salish-53t.1, split out because it changes the DwC-A export and wants verifying against a built archive on its own. Peter's call 2026-09-21: take the register's phylum/class/order/family/genus, but keep emitting kingdom as Animalia rather than NCBI's Metazoa, because a GBIF-facing field should match GBIF's backbone. That inconsistency is deliberate and must be recorded so nobody 'fixes' it later.
acceptance_criteria: All 20,952 exported records still export: dwc.occurrences INNER JOINs taxa_classification, so a taxon missing from the view drops its occurrences from the archive rather than leaving them unclassified. Specifically: (1) the four subspecies with no register entity — Orcinus orca ater (4,707), O. o. rectipinnus (222), Phoca vitulina richardii (20), Eumetopias jubatus monteriensis (2) — resolve through their species; (2) the two taxa with no register entity at all, Delphinapterus leucas (1) and Eubalaena (3), keep the iNaturalist walk; (3) row count of dwc.taxa_classification unchanged at 513, and no exported row's phylum..genus changes; (4) kingdom is never 'Metazoa' anywhere in the view, and is 'Animalia' for every taxon an occurrence reaches; (5) the genus gate still suppresses genus for records identified above genus rank. The DwC-A integration test (scripts/dwca/build.test.ts) is the real gate and only runs meaningfully in CI, where ci-seed.sql supplies data.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #479 (f68afb6) together with salish-53t.1's part 1. See decision 047 and salish-53t.1's closing note.

title: animals: 23 nicknames carry the sheet's '*' as part of the name, so our nicknames don't match
description: Filed upstream as https://github.com/salish-sea/animals/issues/36. The reconciliation against register 2026.09.1 reports 23 of our 403 nicknames as 'not-carried'. It is ONE cause, not 23 gaps: the register's import kept the Bigg's sheet's trailing asterisk (its marker for a provisional nickname) as text, so the register has 'Cook*' where we have 'Cook' with status=provisional (scripts/seed/biggs-ids.ts:206 strips it). Both sides read the same sheet. Until fixed upstream and released, a migration that reads nicknames from the register would show 23 animals with an asterisk in their name and lose our provisional status. Nothing to change on this side; re-run scripts/register/reconcile.ts after the fix and expect nicknames 403/403 carried.
close_reason: Tracked upstream in salish-sea/animals#36. Nothing on this side reads nickname strings from the register — profile pages and relatives lists read public.nicknames, and animal_names is used only for ecotype/taxon names — and salish-ox2.5 keeps nicknames ours, so the asterisk blocks nothing here.

title: The date controls stop at 2000; the corpus now reaches 1976
description:
EARLIEST_OBSERVATION_DATE in src/constants.ts is a hardcoded 2000-01-01, and its comment justifies the bound with 'nothing in the corpus predates it by much (earliest occurrence: 2012)'. Decision 041's backfill made that false on 2026-09-18: inaturalist.observations now reaches 1976-02-01 (203014813, an elephant seal at Ano Nuevo). The calendar, the day steppers and the date input all share the bound, so 24 years of newly-ingested history — every sighting from 1976 to 1999 — cannot be navigated to, and the comment now states a fact that is wrong by 36 years.

Two questions, and they are the owner's: should the controls reach the real floor, and should the floor be derived from the data rather than typed in? Deriving it would mean a query at load time for a bound that changes once a year, which is why it is a constant today; the cheaper fix is a correct constant plus a comment that says which fact it encodes.

Note the artifact: min(observed_at) was 1970-01-01 until salish-4bi purged an epoch-zero row, so a derived floor implemented before that fix would have offered a 1970 calendar. Decision 043 covers that.

Found while fixing salish-4bi.
notes: PR #462: measured before deciding. The 24 years below the 2000 floor hold 99 occurrences of ~116,000, so the bound stays and the comment now records what it costs rather than making a claim about the data that goes stale on every backfill. A derived floor would also have pointed the calendar at 1970 until #461 landed. Close when merged.
close_reason: Closed

title: An upstream epoch-zero date makes the mirror's earliest observation meaningless
description: iNaturalist observation 386594579 has observed_on_string 'Wed Dec 31 1969 16:00:00 GMT -0800 (PST)' — new Date(0) in Pacific time. The observer uploaded an elephant seal at Pescadero in July 2026 and the date arrived as epoch zero; iNat stores it as observed and decision 008 makes us mirror what iNat stores, so inaturalist.observations has exactly one row at epoch 0 and min(observed_at) is 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Found during the decision 041 backfill: the genuine earliest observation is 1976-02-01 (203014813, Ano Nuevo). Anything deriving the depth of the record — a presence grid, an 'earliest sighting', the DwC-A eventDate range — reads the artifact instead. Undecided: whether to filter at ingest (breaks the mirror contract), flag on read, or leave it. Only one row known today; a check for others across sources has not been run.
notes: Fixed in PR #461 (branch fix/epoch-zero-observation-date). Decision 043: epoch-zero is treated as undated and skipped at ingest, beside the existing time_observed_at=null skip; the one row held is purged in migration 20260918200000. Premise correction: filtering at ingest does NOT breach decision 008 — 036 already adjudicated that (008 constrains mirror COLUMNS, not which rows the mirror holds), and a read-time filter would leave min(observed_at) at 1970 anyway, which is the complaint. Cross-source check now run: only iNaturalist has an epoch row; maplify begins 2014-04-20, happywhale 2012-07-11, public.observations 2025-06-16. Two suspected consequences are false: the DwC-A eventDate range is 2014-04-20 onward (export has only native+maplify branches, decision 005) and the date controls are floored at a hardcoded 2000-01-01. Follow-up salish-mkz filed: that 2000 floor now hides 24 years of backfilled history. Close when merged.

Run: pnpm exec tsx scripts/backfill/inat-history.ts --source maplify --from 2014-01-01 --to 2022-01-01 --step month. Decision 036's scope rule applies at ingest so the rows land filtered. The kept fraction rises sharply over time under decision 036's scope rule: 13 of ~461 probed for 2014, 285 of ~1,360 for 2020, 734 of ~1,383 for 2021.

title: Precompute occurrences: a maintained table instead of a view plus two five-minute matview refreshes
description:
Every read of the map pays to assemble occurrences from scratch, and every five minutes the database assembles all of them twice to refresh two caches, when about 200 rows have changed. That is the load that made a visitor's 50ms query miss a 3s budget (salish-xfo), and it grows with the archive, not with the day's activity.

What the read path does today: public.occurrences is a four-way UNION ALL view over maplify.sightings, inaturalist.observations, happywhale.encounters and public.observations (sightings reported through SalishSea.io itself). For every row it runs extract_identifiers and extract_travel_direction over the comment text, inaturalist.species_id over the taxon, gis.st_x/st_y over the geography, plus five joins for taxon names, provider, collection and organization. The map's day query is cheap only because an expression index on created_at prunes to a few dozen rows before any of that runs. Then refresh-occurrence-index and refresh-identifier-candidates each scan the whole view — 49k rows, ~7s mean on prod, 32s worst — every five minutes, so about 5% of wall-clock is spent recomputing what was already known.

Proposal: one physical public.occurrences table (or per-source tables under it) holding the derived columns, maintained incrementally by the ingest and by triggers on all four source tables — the native branch included, since a sighting saved through the app must appear on the map at once, not on the next ingest tick. The map reads a plain table with a real index on observed_at and on lon/lat (or a geography index). occurrence_index becomes that table, and occurrence_identifier_candidates derives from it incrementally or on a much slower clock. Both five-minute refreshes go away, and with them the buffer-cache churn and the contention the map's 3s budget keeps losing to.

Decisions that need a record before starting: whether derived text (identifiers, direction) is stored per source row or per occurrence; how a change to a resolver (a new identifier pattern, a renamed taxon) is backfilled — a full rebuild is fine if it is explicit and rare; whether the DwC-A export and the dwc schema read from the new table or keep the view; and what public.occurrences the PostgREST clients see during the cutover, since the frontend, the profile pages and the export all select from it by name.

Related: salish-xfo (the timeouts; #434 and the broadcast fix are the cheap levers), salish-b0v (indexes for the export's join columns — partly moot if the view goes), salish-t3g (the CDN-side precompute epic; this is the database-side step it would build on).
notes: PR #501 (https://github.com/salish-sea/salishsea-io/pull/501), decision 055. Rehearsed on a prod data restore: 63,491 rows, zero drift, migration 6s on laptop. After deploy: verify cron 'rebuild-occurrences-if-stale' runs, occurrence_index refresh gone from pg_stat_statements, temp_bytes growth near zero. Follow-up: salish-ddj (happywhale varchar drift).
close_reason: Merged #501 (f4572bc), deployed 2026-09-28 02:0x UTC. Prod: 63,493 occurrences in derived.occurrences, zero drift vs derivation, candidates 16,228; old refresh jobs gone; rebuild-occurrences-if-stale ran after the register refresh in 17.6s; ingest ticks succeed as the ingest role. Decision 055.

comments.author: Peter Abrahamsen
comments.text: Relation to salish-t3g (precompute the logged-out read path as static artefacts on the CDN, deferred pending the OrcaSound conversation): that epic removes PostgREST from the read side entirely; this issue is the smaller, database-side step — keep the derived rows in a table maintained as sources change, so the view and both matview refreshes go. It stands on its own and it is also the natural source for whatever t3g publishes: a static artefact is easier to cut from a table that is already right than from a view that has to be assembled per request. 🤖

title: Supabase's default privileges still hand writes to anon on every new public table
description:
20260910040000 revoked the write grants that existed. It did not change where they came from: production's ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES still grants anon and authenticated INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER on every table created in `public`.

    prod   default ACL, postgres in public:  anon=arwdDxtm/postgres
    local  default ACL, postgres in public:  anon=Dxtm/postgres

So the next `CREATE TABLE public.<anything>` reopens the same situation for that table, in prod only, invisibly from a laptop. That is exactly how salish-5of's feedback table shipped with a hole a client could use to make its own report invisible.

There is a guard in the meantime, and it is why this is P2 rather than P1: `supabase/public-grants.test.ts` asserts that anon holds *zero* table write privileges in `public`, so a new table inheriting the permissive default fails CI rather than reaching production quietly. The guard catches it; the default still causes it.

The fix is a migration doing roughly:

    ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER ON TABLES FROM anon, authenticated;

Not done in 20260910040000 deliberately: it changes the behaviour of every future table, the default is per-granting-role (`postgres` and `supabase_admin` both carry one), and tables created through the Supabase dashboard rather than a migration may depend on it. That wants checking rather than assuming, and its own decision — the tightening is right, but "which role's defaults, and what breaks" is unanswered.

Do it alongside a note in the README convention, which already says SELECT grants ship in the migration that creates a table. Once defaults are narrow, the same becomes true of write grants, and that is the point: a table's permissions should be something a migration says, not something the schema hands out.

comments.author: Peter Abrahamsen
comments.text: Correction to the description above: the interim guard checks BOTH roles, not just anon. supabase/public-grants.test.ts asserts anon holds zero table write privileges in public AND that authenticated's write list is exactly observations/observation_photos × INSERT,UPDATE,DELETE — so a new table inheriting the permissive default fails CI whichever role it lands on. Verified by granting writes on public.individuals to both roles: both assertions fail. 🤖

title: The feedback widget could not send, and took the report with it
description:
Scott tried twice on 2026-09-08 (15:11 and 15:12 PDT) to send feedback from an iPhone on Safari, and both times the Sentry widget answered: "Unable to send feedback. This could be because of network issues, or because you are using an ad-blocker." The report never arrived. It survives only because he screenshotted it before giving up, and it is the source of salish-8q9, salish-16b and salish-jo5 — three real bugs that we came within one screenshot of never hearing about.

His text, verbatim, since this is now the only copy:

> Trouble uploading pix for Jpod and today, on both cellular and SeaTac WiFi. Also could not delete all photos from a cloned observation. Will file issue if these continue, but wanted to flag new behavior (& test feedback megaphone UI!)

He was testing the feedback button on purpose. It failed the test.

What is ruled out: **CSP is not the cause.** `index.html` already lists `https://o4509634382331904.ingest.us.sentry.io` in `connect-src`, matching the DSN host in src/sentry.ts.

What is consistent with the evidence: Sentry was unreachable from that device. There are **zero** Sentry events from anyone in the two hours either side (2026-09-08 21:30–23:30 UTC, errors dataset). That is weak evidence on its own — the site is quiet and salish-16b means his upload failures would not have reported anyway — but it is what we have. Two candidates, both fitting failure on cellular *and* SeaTac WiFi, which rules out one flaky network:
- An iOS content blocker. Sentry ingest hosts appear on common tracker blocklists, so a blocker suppresses every Sentry request regardless of network. Sentry's own message puts this first for a reason.
- SeaTac's captive portal for the WiFi half, though that does not explain the cellular half.

The deeper problem is not which one it was. It is that **the only channel a contributor has for telling us something is broken depends on a third-party host that may be blocked, and it discards their text when it fails.** Scott had typed a paragraph; the widget kept it on screen but could not deliver it, and offered him nothing else to do with it.

Worth deciding:
- A fallback that does not depend on sentry.io — the report is small, and we already have a Supabase the app is talking to anyway. A `feedback` table would be reachable whenever the rest of the app is.
- Failing that, at minimum do not lose the text: offer a copy-to-clipboard or a `mailto:` prefilled with what they wrote, so a failed send degrades to a manual send instead of a dead end.

This wants a decision record either way, since it changes who we depend on to hear from users. It sits alongside decision 031, which made sure *failures* reach both audiences; this is the same argument one level up, for the channel people use deliberately.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #436, merged as 1ce870c. Feedback posts to public.feedback via submit_feedback; the draft survives a failed send; feedback-notify.yml files each report as a GitHub issue with the message fenced and contact details withheld. Decision 039.
