title: Removing a photo can delete a different one, or appear to do nothing
description:
Scott, 2026-09-08: "could not delete all photos from a cloned observation."

`removePhoto` looks the photo up by object identity and does not check that it found it:

    removePhoto(photo: Photo) {
        const index = this.photos.indexOf(photo);
        this.photos = this.photos.toSpliced(index, 1, {...photo, state: 'removed'});
    }

When `indexOf` returns -1, `toSpliced(-1, 1, x)` does not fail — it **replaces the last element** (verified: `['x','y'].toSpliced(-1,1,'Z')` is `['x','Z']`). So the photo you clicked ❌ on stays exactly where it is, and a photo you said nothing about silently becomes `removed` and vanishes from the strip. Click again and the same thing happens to the new last element. That is what "could not delete all photos" looks like from the outside: the ❌ appears to move photos around instead of deleting them.

The reference comes from the DOM — `(e.target as PhotoAttachment).photo`, set by `.photo=${photo}` in the `repeat()` — so it goes stale whenever `this.photos` is rebuilt with fresh objects while a `<photo-attachment>` still holds the old one. `formDataFromObservation` rebuilds every entry:

    photos: observation.photos.map(photo => ({state: 'attached', thumb: photo.thumb || photo.src, url: photo.src}))

Why a **cloned** observation makes this reachable is worth spelling out. Cloning does `const clone = {...sighting, id: v7()}` (src/salish-sea.ts) — a shallow spread, so the clone and the original share one `photos` array, and the original is still live in the list. Any path that re-derives the form's photos from an observation — a realtime `occurrences_changed` re-fetch, re-entering edit — mints new objects underneath components still holding the old ones. On a fresh sighting there is nothing to re-derive from, which fits the report being specific to a clone.

I have not reproduced this end to end, so treat the clone mechanism as the likely trigger rather than a confirmed one. The -1 hazard itself is not in doubt, and it is worth closing regardless of how the stale reference arises: an identity lookup that misses should be a no-op or a loud failure, never a silent edit to an unrelated row.

Two things to settle together:
- Give photos a stable id minted when added, and key `repeat()` and removal on it rather than on object identity. salish-8q9 needs the same thing for a different reason (an index carried across an await), so they should probably be fixed in one pass.
- Deep-copy on clone, or stop sharing the photos array — sharing it between two live observations is a hazard beyond this bug.

title: One failed ingest tick raises a Sentry error the heartbeat already covers
description:
The ingest cron fires every 5 minutes and refetches a rolling ~10-day window, so a tick that fails is re-covered by the next one five minutes later over exactly the same ground. Nothing is lost and nobody acts. But `supabase/functions/ingest/index.ts` calls `Sentry.captureException` on every failed run, so each of those self-healing ticks files an error report.

A worked example. SALISHSEA-IO-2E (https://beam-reach.sentry.io/issues/SALISHSEA-IO-2E) is `AbortError: The signal has been aborted` from `fetch-maplify.ts:31` — Maplify didn't answer inside the 15s per-attempt deadline, three attempts running. 35 occurrences between 2026-07-08 and 2026-08-31. Over that stretch the cron fired roughly 15,000 times, so we are looking at a ~0.2% upstream failure rate on a fetch that retries and a window that repeats. The run at 2026-08-31 16:35 covered 2026-08-21→08-31; so did the run at 16:40.

We already have the alert that matters, and it is the one Sentry structurally cannot give: `scripts/ingest/heartbeat.ts` trips when no *successful* run for a source is newer than 30 minutes — six consecutive failures — and files a GitHub issue. Its own header says why it exists: "Catches a cron that stopped firing — the gap Sentry can't see, because a job that never runs throws no exception." Sustained failure is covered. The per-tick exception adds a second, noisier channel for the case the first one deliberately declines to fire on.

Three issues are this same shape:
- SALISHSEA-IO-2E — Maplify timeout, 35 events
- SALISHSEA-IO-3C — Maplify connection refused, 1 event
- SALISHSEA-IO-3J — `write EBADF`, the postgres.js socket dying under a query, 1 event

The question to settle: should a failed ingest run capture to Sentry at all, or should the `ingest.runs` row plus the heartbeat be the whole story? Decision 011 (docs/decisions/011-*) put the audit row outside the data transaction so a crash leaves a visible orphan; decision 012 covers the heartbeat. A middle option is to keep the capture but drop the level to `warning`, or to capture only when the failure is *non*-transient (a 403, a persistent non-JSON body) and stay quiet on the retryable classes that the next tick fixes.

Whatever is chosen, it amends how we alert, so it belongs in a decision record rather than a code comment.

All three Sentry issues are ignored-until-escalating pending this.
close_reason: Decision 042 accepted and shipped in PR #460 (9f35b1e). A failed CRON tick the fetch layer already retried is recorded in ingest.runs and not sent to Sentry; defects and ALL manual runs report as before. Transient == what isRetryableStatus already retries, marked where thrown, so one classifier serves retrying and alerting. Blanket silence was rejected on the record: 35 of 89 logged failures were real defects (32 pagination-incomplete, 3 parse/schema) interleaved with successes, so the heartbeat never tripped on them. CodeRabbit caught that the first version suppressed manual runs too, which would have lost a failed backfill silently - the 2018-01 Maplify HTTP 520 shape. SALISHSEA-IO-3K resolved. Follow-up: SALISHSEA-IO-2E and -3C are transient classes and can be resolved; -3J (write EBADF, postgres.js socket) is NOT a fetch failure and stays reported.

title: Sentry has no client-side noise filter, so third-party errors keep arriving
description:
Of the 13 unresolved Sentry issues on 2026-09-09, eight were not defects and four of those were not our code at all — an Android in-app browser's injected analytics bridge, its iOS twin, a visitor's browser extension talking to a dead tab, and a year of opaque "Script error." from cross-origin scripts. Someone has to recognise each one as noise, again, every time it recurs. Ignoring them in the Sentry UI is a per-issue-group answer to a per-error-class problem: SALISHSEA-IO-37, -38 and -3B are three groups for one failure ("Load failed"/"Failed to fetch" on a visitor's connection), and the next release fingerprints them as a fourth.

`src/sentry.ts` configures the client with integrations only — no `ignoreErrors`, no `denyUrls`, no `beforeSend`. That is the gap. The client can decline to send what it can already tell is not about us.

Candidates, all evidenced in the issues above:
- `denyUrls` on `iabjs://` (SALISHSEA-IO-3E) and extension schemes.
- `ignoreErrors` on the in-app-browser bridge messages that get *blamed on salishsea.io* because the host injects the script into our document, so `denyUrls` can't see them (SALISHSEA-IO-3F: `sendDataToNative`, `sendPageShowMessage`, `window.webkit.messageHandlers`).
- "Script error." with no usable frame (SALISHSEA-IO-Q, 241 occurrences).

Decide separately, and don't lump it in: whether client network failures ("Failed to fetch", "Load failed") should be dropped at the client or left to arrive. They are currently ignored-until-escalating in Sentry precisely because volume is the only thing distinguishing a boat losing signal from a Supabase outage or a botched CSP deploy — a client-side filter would throw that signal away. Prefer keeping them and fixing the grouping.

This is a change to what we hear about, so it wants a decision record alongside 037 (docs/decisions/037-sentry-transmits-from-production-only.md), whose rejected-alternatives section already argues the relevant point: filtering in the Sentry UI is not the same as not sending, because ignored events still cost quota and still have to be recognised by whoever opens the list.

Related: salish-ogb (geolocation denial, the one noise class that is our own call site).
close_reason: Closed

title: Geolocation permission denial is not a Sentry error
description:
Someone taps "show my location", their browser asks, they say no, and we file an error report about it. That is the feature working. Sentry has been carrying it as SALISHSEA-IO-3H (https://beam-reach.sentry.io/issues/SALISHSEA-IO-3H) — `Error: [object GeolocationPositionError]`, handled, no stacktrace, nothing anyone can act on.

It gets there honestly. Decision 031 (docs/decisions/031-surfacing-failures.md) coupled the two audiences on purpose: `reportError()` captures to Sentry *and* raises the toast, because the bug that motivated the record had reached neither. Both geolocation call sites — `src/user-location-control.ts` and `sighting-form.ts`'s locateMe — go through it, and `src/geolocation-message.ts` already says the useful thing to the person holding the phone ("your browser is blocking location access for this site").

The coupling is right for a failed *action* and wrong for a *withheld permission*. PERMISSION_DENIED (code 1) is a choice the visitor is entitled to make; POSITION_UNAVAILABLE (2) and TIMEOUT (3) are the device failing, which is at least arguably worth counting.

The work: let a caller tell the toast without telling Sentry, and use it for code 1 at both sites. Then amend 031 to record the exception and why — the record's whole argument is that the two halves travel together, so an exception to it belongs in the record rather than as an undocumented flag.

Open: whether 2 and 3 stay reportable. They are not defects either, but unlike a denial they can indicate something real (a device with no fix, a timeout we chose at 5s in sighting-form).
close_reason: Merged in PR #448: reportError takes capture:false; geolocationErrorIsReportable excludes PERMISSION_DENIED at both call sites; non-Error causes wrapped for Sentry; decision 031 amended.

title: Smoke tests race Lambda@Edge replication, so a good deploy goes red
description:
Every deploy that republishes the Lambda@Edge OG handler can fail its own smoke test and file a spurious deploy-failed issue, which trains us to ignore both.

OBSERVED 2026-08-31, run 33357057846 (commit 4dbb672, PR #420). Build, Test and Deploy all passed — production was updated. Smoke failed: a bot UA fetching /individuals/T065A got the generic shell, <title>Individual — SalishSea.io</title>, with no per-individual OG tags. That is decision 015's documented fail-open path, taken because the new function version had not yet replicated to the edge location serving the request. Lambda@Edge replication takes minutes; the smoke job starts as soon as Deploy returns.

Not a regression in the merged change: it touched 13 files, all under src/ and docs/, none of them the edge handler, individual.html or anything on the OG path. curl with a bot UA a few minutes later returned the full tags (og:title 'Fingers (T065A)'), and re-running the failed job passed with no code change.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE RED RUN. The failure path files a GitHub issue via the Alert-on-failure job (this one filed #421, auto-closed on re-run). A check that cries wolf on a healthy deploy is worse than no check: the next real OG regression looks like the flake we have learned to re-run.

OPTIONS, none chosen:
- Retry the OG assertions with a bounded poll (e.g. up to ~3 min) before failing — smallest change, keeps the assertion honest, just stops it from asserting too early.
- Have the deploy job wait for the edge function to report replicated before handing off to smoke.
- Split the OG checks into a separate job that is allowed to be slow, keeping the fast smoke checks (homepage 200 etc.) strict.

Files: .github/workflows/smoke.yml, e2e/og-previews.spec.ts, decision 015.
acceptance_criteria: A deploy that republishes the edge handler does not fail smoke, and does not file a deploy-failed issue, purely because replication has not finished. A genuine OG regression still fails.
close_reason: Merged in PR #447: og-previews.spec.ts waits up to 5 minutes for the edge handler to answer with profile tags before asserting; smoke step timeout 8m; runbook notes it.

comments.author: Peter Abrahamsen
comments.text: Chosen: the bounded poll, as a readiness wait separate from the assertions (PR #447). e2e/og-previews.spec.ts probes /individuals/T065A with a bot UA every 10s for up to 5 minutes before running its specs unchanged, so a real regression still fails with the assertion's own message. Rejected: waiting on replication in the deploy job (no clean signal from AWS) and a separate slow OG job (moves the flake rather than removing it). 🤖

title: Decide whether iNaturalist gets the same ingest scope rule
description:
Decision 036 applies 'killer whales range-wide, everything else the Salish Sea' to Maplify and purges 14,146 rows. iNaturalist fetches the SAME Acartia box (scripts/ingest/inaturalist.ts SALISH_SEA_BBOX = -136,36,-120,54 — mislabelled 'Salish Sea') with no place filter, so it holds Californian humpbacks, sea lions (decision 009 counts ~2,150) and otters exactly as Maplify did. After 036 a Maplify humpback in Monterey Bay is purged while the iNaturalist one beside it stays; the Everywhere region and PRODUCT.md's spatial-scope statement are only true for Maplify.

Options: (a) apply the same predicate to iNaturalist observations at ingest plus a one-time purge — symmetry, and the product statement becomes true for the whole corpus; (b) leave iNaturalist wide — its non-cetacean records are the archive's only unique non-cetacean contribution (027), though the Californian ones are not a Salish Sea contribution; (c) apply the rule to cetaceans only and keep wide pinnipeds/otters. Undecided; owner's call. Whichever way, rename SALISH_SEA_BBOX to what it is (acartiaExtent from src/extents.ts) so the mislabel stops misleading — it already misled decision 036's first draft.

Measure first: count iNat observations outside salishSeaExtent by taxon before deciding.
notes:
Decided: apply 036's rule to iNaturalist (option a), owner confirmed 2026-09-18. PR #463.

Measurement the bead asked for, against prod: 81,785 observations, 51,637 out of scope (63%, vs 35% for Maplify), 30,148 kept. 42,493 of the doomed rows are Californian; Pier 39 SF alone is 1,894. Steady state, not backlog: 863 of the last 1,873 ingested were Californian. By group outside the box: 34,376 pinnipeds, 11,851 cetaceans (905 orca kept), 6,311 otters.

027's counter-argument does not survive contact with the data: 17,563 pinniped + 4,787 otter records are INSIDE the box and untouched, so the unique non-cetacean contribution is intact. Option (c) (cetaceans only) is backwards — drops 10,946 cetaceans, keeps 40,687 Californian pinnipeds/otters.

Implementation: isIngestable in the iNat core reads the record's ancestry for genus Orcinus (41520) — exact, unlike Maplify's name regex. Purge migration 20260918210000 walks inaturalist.taxa down from the genus for the same closure. SALISH_SEA_BBOX renamed FETCH_BBOX from acartiaExtent (the mislabel the bead asked about). Decision 044 written; 036 amended with the superseded bullet struck through.

Cost named in the record: 2,573 rows north of 50.5 go, incl. Johnstone Strait humpbacks; orcas there are kept. Close when merged.

title: Admit coextensive closeMatch to the view; delete SUBSPECIES_FORMS; amend 033
description:
The last step, and the only one in this repo. Once the register carries the
crosswalks, teach the view to use them and delete our stand-in.

RE-STATE THE VIEW'S RULE, don't break it. register.inaturalist_taxon_name
filters `predicate_id = 'skos:exactMatch'` (migration 20260828100000), and the
recorded reason is that a broader match "would put a wider claim on the map
than the data supports". Between coextensive concepts that reason does not
apply. The rule the reason actually describes is EXCLUDE broadMatch — so the
filter becomes a deny-list of widening predicates rather than an allow-list of
one. Write it that way, with the reason next to it, or the next person will
read the change as the rule being relaxed.

Watch the DISTINCT ON tie-break while doing it. The view is unique per iNat
taxon id by luck rather than by design (its own comment says so); admitting a
second predicate widens the space in which two entities can claim one taxon,
and a duplicate there silently DOUBLES every occurrence of that animal on the
map. The animals crosswalk check is the place to catch it, but confirm the
view's ordering still makes the outcome deterministic.

THEN DELETE SUBSPECIES_FORMS from src/symbology.ts. It exists only because the
register could not hold these two animals; once it can, keeping it would be the
second opinion decision 033 forbids. Its tests go with it — but keep `a
resident subspecies is not narrowed to Southern Resident` (salish-frk), which
tests labelForSegment and is unrelated.

Also re-check migration 20260828120000's Orcinus exemption. It exempts the two
orca subspecies from the species roll-up because their qualifier is the ecotype
the map wants; once the ecotype resolves through the register that reasoning
still holds, but the comment explaining it will be stale.

RECORD IT. This amends decision 033, which states the exactMatch-only rule as
settled. The record should carry the SMM quotation, because "an authority
equates these two concepts" is the entire licence for the change, and should
note that the rank dispute (SMM subspecies-provisional vs Bain/Morin/ITIS/CoL
species) is deliberately not resolved by it.

EXPECTED: register coverage 91.5% -> ~99.3% (63,640 of 64,097). Verify against
prod after deploy, the same way 033's figure was.

Blocked on both animals steps.
notes:
2026-09-21 00:5x UTC: animals 2026.09.3 RELEASED and LOADED IN PROD. register.edition = 2026.09.3, SSA:0000003 carries common name 'Resident killer whale', 4 closeMatch mappings present. Measured against the real loaded register: prod is live at 90.42% (56,951/62,987) and reaches 99.71% (62,804) the moment #477 deploys. #477 marked ready for review; awaiting CodeRabbit's PR-side review and Peter's go-ahead to merge, since merging deploys and applies the migration.

TAGGING GOTCHA, cost nothing this time but nearly did: Peter's local ../animals was 2 commits stale when he ran 'git tag 2026.09.3 && git push'. Had the tag not already existed (I created it at main head 387f6ea via the GitHub API), it would have pointed at 26a1e72 — a commit WITHOUT the SSA:0000003 row. The release would have built, published and loaded with no error anywhere, and coverage would have sat at 92.00% with nothing to explain why. Git's refusal to move an existing tag is the only thing that caught it. Tag from the remote SHA, or pull first.
close_reason:
Shipped and verified in production 2026-09-21. PR #477 (2916d98) + animals#39 released as 2026.09.3.

VERIFIED IN PROD, not projected: register coverage 62,804/62,987 = 99.71%, up from 90.42%. Orcinus orca ater -> 'Resident killer whale' (SSA:0000003, 4,856), O. o. rectipinnus -> "Bigg's killer whale" (SSA:0000002, 808), Phocoidea -> 'Pinniped' (SSA:0000938, 189). SUBSPECIES_FORMS deleted; nothing in this repo composes an animal name any more.

The 183-record residue (0.29%) is NOT subspecies and is not this issue: genus and family stubs whose iNaturalist vernacular is a plural or clade description — 'Steller Sea Lions' (51), 'New World River Otters' (14), 'California, Galapagos, and Japanese Sea Lions' (13), 'Oceanic Dolphins and Porpoises' (11), Orcinus with no vernacular at all (9). Decision 033 named these as needing a different answer. Parent salish-0gb can close or be rescoped to them.

TWO CORRECTIONS THIS ISSUE'S OWN TEXT NEEDED. (1) It predicted ~99.3% from the view change alone; the true figure was 92.00%, because the view inner-joins names on type='common' and SSA:0000003 had only its label. animals#39 was unplanned work. (2) It proposed the filter as a deny-list; 'predicate_id IN (...)' is an ALLOW-LIST, and the fail-closed property the issue wanted is the allow-list's, not a deny-list's. CodeRabbit caught that I had carried the wrong word into the code and docs. NOT IN ('skos:broadMatch') would admit narrowMatch, relatedMatch and anything the register adds later; supabase/register-crosswalk.test.ts fails against it.

title: animals: closeMatch the two ecotypes to iNaturalist's subspecies
description:
Once Q1 lands, crosswalk the two ecotypes to iNaturalist's subspecies:

  SSA:0000003 (Resident)  skos:closeMatch  inaturalist.taxon:1602531  (O. o. ater)
  SSA:0000002 (Bigg's)    skos:closeMatch  inaturalist.taxon:1602533  (O. o. rectipinnus)

closeMatch, not exactMatch: the register calls one an ecotype and iNaturalist
calls the other a subspecies, so they are different KINDS of thing with the
same extension. Not broadMatch — that is the predicate for SSA:0000001 ->
NCBITaxon:9733, where the ecotype really is narrower than the target, and it is
the predicate the consuming view must keep excluding.

The justification to carry in the mapping's note column, because it is the
whole reason this is admissible under ADR-0008: the Society for Marine
Mammalogy's 2024 Taxonomy Committee review declined Morin et al.'s species
proposal and wrote that "the two ecotypes are considered provisionally as
distinct subspecies of Orcinus orca". The equation of ecotype with subspecies
is SMM's, not ours.

Do NOT crosswalk SSA:0000010 (Southern Resident community) to `ater`. `ater` is
the resident subspecies generally; the community is one population within it.
That is a broadMatch and it is exactly the narrowing salish-frk removed.

Blocked on the Q1 work.
notes: 2026-09-20: built on branch ecotype-closematch in a SEPARATE WORKTREE (/Users/rainhead/dev/animals-wt-ecotype-closematch) because another agent is working in ../animals. Both iNat taxa verified live (1602531 ater, 1602533 rectipinnus, both subspecies under 41521). CORRECTION to this issue's quotation: SMM's List of Marine Mammal Species and Subspecies (April 2026) says 'the two ecotypes are considered HERE provisionally as distinct subspecies of Orcinus orca' -- the word 'here' was missing above, and the source is the List, not only the 2024 annual review. The rows quote it exactly. Also added a validator check: an external id may be an exact or close match of only ONE entity (the uniqueness salish-0gb.3 worried about, enforced at the source).

title: [bug] The map labels every resident killer whale SRKW, including Northern Residents
description:
src/symbology.ts:194-195. When no prose names a pod or an ecotype,
labelForSegment falls back to the taxon and returns 'SRKW' for every occurrence
filed as Orcinus orca ater.

That is a wider claim than the record supports, and it is the exact error
salish-0gb warns about in the opposite direction. iNaturalist's ater is the
RESIDENT subspecies generally — Southern, Northern and Alaskan residents all —
while SRKW is one population within it. A record that says only "resident
killer whale" is being relabelled as a Southern Resident by us.

MEASURED (2026-08-29, production): 4,377 occurrences carry ater. 44 of them are
already outside the Salish Sea band — 17 north of 49.5 deg, which is Northern
Resident water, and 27 south of 47 deg. Those are the ones where the label is
most likely to be simply false.

It gets worse by design, not better: salish-a4y scopes ingest to killer whales
RANGE-WIDE, so Northern and Alaskan resident records are expected to grow.

THE FIX IS SMALL: return 'Resident' (or 'Resident killer whale') for ater, and
leave 'SRKW' to the prose detector, which only fires when a report actually said
so. detectEcotype already handles that path and runs first. Note the Biggs
branch one line up is fine — rectipinnus and Bigg's are the same population,
so no narrowing happens there.

Where the same names reach other surfaces without going through
labelForSegment, see salish-0gb: obs-summary.ts:200 and the two card renderers
show iNaturalist's 'Resident Killer Whale' verbatim.
notes: Fixed in #412, merged as 0dc3ade and deployed 2026-08-29. labelForSegment returns 'Resident' for Orcinus orca ater; prose naming a pod or ecotype still wins, so a report saying 'southern residents' still reads SRKW. Verified live in the production bundle. Pinned by test 'a resident subspecies is not narrowed to Southern Resident'.
close_reason: Closed

title: Materialize register individuals and groups; public.* stops asserting identity
description:
The schema work: load the register's individual and group entities, their names,
memberships and parentage into Postgres, and make public.* read identity from there
rather than assert it.

STATUS 2026-09-20 -- nothing external blocks this any more. The four blockers it was filed with are all resolved: the URL scheme is decided and shipped for individuals and ecotypes (salish-ox2.2, decision 034); the six name-only named_group shells are retired (salish-ox2.3); the sub-matriline question is settled by the register minting the 73 sub-lineages ahead of Q22 (salish-ox2.6, edition 2026.09.1, loaded in production); and the reconciliation has been re-run against that edition (salish-ox2.1 / salishsea-io#474: 133 of 133 groups and 510 of 510 individuals matched). DONE SO FAR: every individual, the ecotype and every matriline carries its register identifier (#418, #475). REMAINING: move /matrilines/ to identifier-keyed URLs (decision 034); load register membership and read group membership from it rather than from our own rows (see the notes on how a matriarch is encoded); retire what public.* then no longer needs to assert. Q22 staying open is not a blocker: its answer confirms the sub-lineages or retires them.

Decision 035 makes this issue the gate for Orcasound production tag-writing
(salish-8vr.24), so its completion date matters to another epic.

Note the split decision 034 created: the URL cutover is NOT all-or-nothing with this
issue. /individuals/ and /ecotypes/ adopt identifier-keyed URLs as soon as
public.individuals carries SSA: (510/510 and 1/1 reconciled); only /matrilines/ waits
on the group half.

Shape, following what salish-ayb.5 already established:

• The register schema exists and is loaded (migration 20260828100000,
scripts/register/load.ts, edition recorded with its digest). This extends
it to entities of kind individual and group, plus membership.tsv and
parentage.tsv — not a new mechanism.
• public.* carries SSA: directly. No animals mirror schema, no translation
layer: decision 008 does not govern the register (decision 033).
• Names resolve through the register the way taxon names now do, and display
stays ours to compose (ADR-0011).
• The catalogue tables do not simply drop. individuals.taxon_id, the
provenance edges, the nickname stories and namers, and parties are ours and
stay; what goes is the second opinion about which animals exist.
• A graceful fallback here is more dangerous than for names. salish-1g8 is
about an empty register reading as "no name for this animal"; an empty
register reading as "this whale does not exist" would blank profile pages.

title: Decide the sequencing against Orcasound tagging (ADR-0012's open question)
description:
ADR-0012 asks it and does not answer it: "What is the migration sequence, and
does the catalogue migrate before or after the first Orcasound bout is tagged?
Tagging against identifiers that later change would defeat the purpose."

This epic and salish-8vr are therefore order-dependent, and neither currently
says which goes first. The question is live now rather than theoretical:
salish-8vr.9 (register-aware tag picker on bouts) and salish-8vr.7 (kind + iri
on tags) are the point at which Orcasound starts writing SSA: identifiers down.

The asymmetry that probably settles it: Orcasound tagging against the register
is SAFE whenever it happens, because ADR-0002 makes SSA: identifiers opaque and
permanent and ADR-0010 forbids reuse. What is unsafe is Orcasound tagging
against OUR designations, or us continuing to mint identity Orcasound might
adopt. If that holds, the sequencing constraint is weaker than ADR-0012 feared
and the two can proceed in parallel — but say so deliberately rather than by
default.

Record the answer where both epics can see it. Decision 028 makes SalishSea.io
the single voice recommending a schema to Orcasound, so this is our call to
make and communicate.
notes:
DECIDED 2026-08-30: before. Recorded as docs/decisions/035-catalogue-migrates-before-tagging.md.

The asymmetry this issue floated (parallel is safe because SSA: is permanent) holds for
individuals and fails for groups -- and a bout tag is usually a group, which is the tier Q22
(animals#13) has open and the register calls its least confident. The identifiers would not
change; the level a moderator tags at might not exist yet. So the first production bout tag
waits for ox2.5, recorded in the graph as salish-8vr.9 blocked-by salish-ox2.5.

Not blocked meanwhile: orcasite#1013 (kind+iri), building #1015's picker, the 94-tag
classification. Named fallback if Q22 stalls: a picker scoped to individuals+ecotypes
(510/510 and 1/1 reconciled). Communicate on orcasite#1015 when the picker approaches merge.
GRAPH CORRECTION 2026-08-30: the edge is now salish-8vr.24 (activation) blocked-by salish-ox2.5,
not salish-8vr.9 -- CodeRabbit pointed out the original edge gated building the picker, which 035
explicitly permits. 035 amended in the same PR (#417).

title: Retire the six empty named_group rows; findings 1 and 4 are answered
description:
Both halves of this issue's original premise were measured empty by salish-ox2.1, so it is
no longer a question to carry upstream. What remains is our own cleanup, and that cleanup
does still block salish-ox2.5.

WHAT CHANGED

Finding 1 (membership_basis = association, animals Q15): 375 of 375 membership rows are
maternal. Zero association rows. Nothing to negotiate.

Finding 4 (named_group has no rank and the register's validator requires one): the register
already expresses these, as a `common` name on the ranked matriline. And on our side, all
six named_group rows have zero members, no anchor_individual_id and no parent_group_id --
measured in prod 2026-08-30. ADR-0012 says we hold real travelling groups the validator
cannot accept. We do not. We hold six empty rows holding a name that also lives on the
matriline.

Carried upstream as evidence on Q22 part (c), animals#13:
https://github.com/salish-sea/animals/issues/13#issuecomment-5469771413

WHY THIS STILL BLOCKS salish-ox2.5

Those six rows are the collisions the reconciliation found: each register entity is claimed
by two of our rows, the named_group and the matriline it names.

  SSA:0002001 T007s  <- Secret Agents + T007
  SSA:0002009 T023s  <- Motley Crew + T023
  SSA:0002020 T041s  <- Ted's Gang + T041
  SSA:0002039 T073s  <- Sea Monster Family + T073
  SSA:0002049 T099s  <- Gretzky's + T099
  SSA:0002054 T109s  <- Runaway's + T109

A migration assigning identifiers row by row would hand both rows the same SSA: and not
notice. So the retirement has to happen before ox2.5 materializes groups, which is why the
blocking dependency stays.

THE WORK

Retire the six named_group rows, and carry their names as nicknames on the matriline they
name -- which is where the register puts them and where our own rosters already are.
Confirm nothing references them first: they have no memberships, but check occurrence
identifications and any UI that lists social_groups by kind.

Refs: salish-ox2.1 (docs/reference/register-reconciliation.md), animals ADR-0012 finding 4,
ADR-0005, Q15 (animals#11), Q22 (animals#13).
notes:
MEASURED BY salish-ox2.1 (2026-08-30, edition 2026.08.1 in production). Both findings
this issue carries upstream have changed shape. Do not open the upstream conversation
on the original framing.

FINDING 1 IS ZERO ROWS. All 375 group_memberships are basis=maternal; none are
association. ADR-0012 framed this as an unbounded risk — "how many are association
decides how much of our data has nowhere to go" under ADR-0005 — and the answer is
none of it. Q15 (salish-sea/animals#11) still deserves an answer for the register's
own sake, but it does not block this migration and should not be presented as though
it does.

FINDING 4 IS ALREADY SOLVED UPSTREAM, differently than assumed. The framing was "a
named_group is a real travelling group with a name and no rank, and the register's
validator requires a rank". But edition 2026.08.1 already carries all six of ours —
as a `common` NAME on the ranked matriline, not as a group:

  SSA:0002001  T007s  matriline   name "Secret Agents"  (common)
  SSA:0002009  T023s  matriline   name "Motley Crew"    (common)
  SSA:0002020  T041s  ... Ted's Gang / SSA:0002039 Sea Monster Family
  SSA:0002049  Gretzky's / SSA:0002054 Runaway's

So the register never needed a rankless group. The real question to carry upstream is
narrower and more answerable: IS THAT DELIBERATE, or an artefact of how the source
sheet's "Known as" headings were read? If deliberate, our named_group rows are not
entities at all on the register's model and salish-ox2.5 should migrate them to names,
not to identifiers. If accidental, the register has six collective names attached to
the wrong kind of thing.

Either way it is a collision on our side: those six matrilines are each claimed by TWO
catalogue rows (the named_group and the matriline), which is the one finding that
would make a row-by-row identifier assignment silently wrong.

A THIRD THING TO CARRY, not previously on this issue: our 132 matrilines and the
register's 132 Bigg's matrilines overlap in only 59. We subdivide (T073A, T064B1); the
register has NO letter-suffixed matriline at all, only top-level prefixes (T073s), and
its own rows say the grouping is unconfirmed pending animals Q22. That is a question
for the same conversation.

MEASURED 2026-08-30 (prod): all six named_group rows have zero members, no anchor_individual_id
and no parent_group_id. They are name-only shells -- Secret Agents, Motley Crew, Ted's Gang, Sea
Monster Family, Gretzky's, Runaway's.

So finding 4 does not need carrying upstream as a requirement at all. ADR-0012 says we hold real
travelling groups with a name and no rank that the register's validator cannot accept. We do not
hold them. The roster lives on the matriline in our data too; we wrote the name down twice, and
the reconciliation caught all six colliding with the matriline they name.

The register's choice -- the collective name as a 'common' name on the ranked lineage entity -- is
therefore where both sides actually put the animals. What remains for this issue is our own
cleanup: six redundant rows to retire, not a vocabulary gap to negotiate. That belongs with
salish-ox2.6/animals#13 (Q22 part c) rather than as a standalone question.

Finding 1 (association membership) was already sized to zero by salish-ox2.1. This issue's
original premise is now empty on both halves; reframe or close it.
PR salishsea-io#418 (branch ox2-cleanup-and-slice): migration 20260830120000 moves the six
names onto their matrilines (stories and themes intact) and deletes the shells, guarded
against a shell that acquired data since the measurement. Seed parser no longer mints
named_group rows -- a 'Known as' heading becomes a nickname on the lineage root it heads.
Visible change: six matriline pages now show their community name. Close on merge.

title: Ingest heartbeat can miss a transient outage entirely
description:
Found while triaging GH #378 (2026-08-29).

Both ingest sources gapped for 60 minutes on 2026-08-28, 15:50 -> 16:50 UTC — twice the 30-minute staleness threshold — and no alert was filed. GH #378 was never updated (updated_at still equals created_at), so the heartbeat never observed it: gh run list shows exactly one ingest-heartbeat run between 14:30 and 18:00, at 17:35, by which time the gap had healed.

Cause is the observer's own cadence, not its logic. The workflow is scheduled '*/30' and GitHub's scheduled cron is best-effort — it skipped the runs that would have covered the window. The workflow comment says lateness 'only delays detection, never falsifies it'; that holds for an ONGOING outage but not for a transient one that heals between two checks. A 60-minute outage can therefore be invisible.

Worth considering:
- Measure against the worst gap since the last check, not just current staleness — ingest.runs retains the history, so a check at T can see that a >30m gap occurred at any point since T-1 even if things are fresh now.
- That makes detection independent of when the observer happens to run, which is the property the current design assumes it already has.

Note also that the workflow reuses a single open 'ingest-heartbeat-failed' issue (updating rather than opening), so a stale open alert suppresses new ones — #378 sat open for 18 days after healing.
close_reason: Merged in PR #449: heartbeat.ts adds a gap check over a 24h lookback (any interval between successes > freshness), the workflow closes the alert issue on a passing check, decision 012 amended with the measured cadence (median 68m, max 12.5h).

title: [epic] Precompute the logged-out read path as static artefacts
description:
DEFERRED pending a consolidation conversation with Orcasound — see the SSO note at the
bottom, which is the actual gate.

THE IDEA. Everything a logged-out visitor loads is derivable and changes at most every few
minutes, yet today it is recomputed per request through PostgREST — including
occurrence_days, which recounts every day in a range on every page load. Precompute it to
object storage and serve it from the CDN.

WHY IT COMES BEFORE ANY MIGRATION, not after. The exit from Supabase (salish-9uu) is hard
because RLS + auth.uid() + PostgREST together ARE the backend. Precomputing the read path
removes PostgREST from the read side entirely, and what remains is a small write API —
an ordinary thing to build on any host. It shrinks the migration rather than being
sequenced around it.

AND IT ANSWERS THE OUTAGE DIRECTLY. On 2026-08-28 the database stopped accepting
connections and salishsea.io served nothing to anyone. With a precomputed read path,
logged-out visitors would not have noticed. That is a stronger availability property than
any choice of host, and it is independent of where Postgres ends up living.

FORMAT — three options, and the shape of the win differs

  Per-day JSON. One file per day; the client filters by region locally, so regions do not
  multiply the cardinality at all. ~50-100 occurrences a day, ~3,650 files for a decade,
  a few KB each. Simplest to generate and invalidate; a 5-minute ingest rewrites only the
  days it touched. But every new view (profiles, calendar, arbitrary ranges) needs its own
  precomputed shape, so the design keeps growing.

  Gzipped SQLite. One artefact the client queries arbitrarily — day views, calendar
  counts, individual and group profiles, all from the same file, with no per-view design
  work. Range-request techniques (sql.js-httpvfs and similar) avoid downloading the whole
  thing. The corpus is ~64k occurrences, so this is small.

  Parquet + DuckDB-wasm. Same "one artefact, arbitrary queries" advantage, better at
  columnar aggregation, and it is already in the stack — scripts/dwca uses DuckDB.

The owner reports success shipping both SQLite and Parquet on other projects. The real
distinction is not file size: per-day JSON forces a precomputed shape per view, while
SQLite and Parquet move the query to the client and stop that treadmill. Weigh that
against staleness granularity and the cost of regenerating one artefact every few minutes
versus rewriting a handful of day files.

OPEN QUESTIONS
  - How a 5-minute ingest invalidates only what changed.
  - What happens to the realtime channel now driving map refresh. It may simply become
    "re-fetch today's artefact".
  - Whether the write path keeps PostgREST + RLS, or becomes a small explicit API.

THE GATE: SSO. Consolidating infrastructure with Orcasound raises shared identity, and
that is the pivot for all of this rather than a side question. The auth.uid() shim that
makes salish-9uu's option 2 tractable assumes WE mint the JWTs. If identity becomes shared
across sites, that assumption is not ours to make alone, and the hardest part of leaving
Supabase — 16 migrations and 10 RLS policy files built on auth.uid() — is decided by that
conversation.

Worth noting the parallel: the animals register already solved shared identity for the
ANIMALS both projects talk about. It does not transfer to people. ADR-0014 frames the
register as a publication consumed at a pinned tag, which works precisely because animal
identity changes slowly; a session cannot be consumed at a pinned tag.
notes: 2026-09-27 (Peter): the Orcasound SSO conversation gates only the LATER steps (the write path and auth), not this epic's read path. Precomputing the logged-out reads, serving them, and moving ingest into a build graph never touch who issues login tokens, so they can proceed ahead of that conversation. Share links (?o=<id>) keep their current Supabase lookup in the interim; the static answer is still to be designed, with the constraint that the URL in the address bar must remain the shareable link (no 'copy link' button people have to find).
close_reason: All 15 children closed 2026-10-06. The logged-out read path is static files built by Stelis on the Fly machine (decisions 056, 057, 061), prerendered profile pages included; the Fly app deploys from GitHub Actions on every merge (t3g.5, .10) with a clean shutdown (decision 066) and the Stelis pin in fly/stelis-commit (t3g.9). Open follow-up elsewhere: salish-v6xq.

title: Decide the target architecture for leaving Supabase
description:
Write the decision record choosing among self-hosted Supabase on Fly, Fly Postgres +
PostgREST + our own auth, or a conventional backend API.

MUST RESOLVE
  - Whether decision 002 (static SPA, no backend) still holds. Everything else follows
    from that answer. If it holds, PostgREST stays and auth.uid() needs a shim. If it
    does not, the exit is a rewrite and should be planned as one.
  - What replaces GoTrue for Google sign-in, and whether it mints JWTs whose claims
    satisfy the existing RLS policies unchanged.
  - Whether Realtime survives. It is one broadcast channel driving map refresh; a
    polling fallback may be cheaper than running Realtime.
  - Where the ingest runs once pg_cron and pg_net are gone.
  - What the DwC-A build connects to.
  - What we lose: PITR, automated backups, the dashboard. These are real and should be
    priced rather than waved at.

Do not start this while the outage is fresh. A migration chosen in irritation is a
migration regretted.

title: [epic] Exit plan: leaving Supabase, likely for Fly.io
description:
Prompted by a production outage on 2026-08-28: the database stopped accepting connections,
salishsea.io rendered empty for users, and we could not even inspect pg_stat_activity to
see why. Supabase's own API reported the project ACTIVE_HEALTHY throughout. orcasite is
likely moving to Fly.io, which makes Fly the natural target.

THE ARGUMENT IS CONTROL, NOT COST. A self-hosted stack has its own failure modes and will
sometimes be worse. What it gives is the ability to look: today we could not list running
queries, could not kill a suspect one, and had no signal beyond a status page that
disagreed with reality. For a project whose whole value is being a reliable record, being
unable to diagnose is the sharper problem.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY COUPLED (measured 2026-08-28, not estimated)

  PostgREST    ~19 call sites across 12 relations and 2 RPCs (upsert_observation,
               occurrence_days). This is the defining dependency: decision 002 makes this
               a static SPA with NO backend, so PostgREST *is* the backend.
  Auth         4 client methods (signInWithIdToken for Google, getUser,
               onAuthStateChange, signOut) and 16 migrations referencing auth.uid() or
               auth.users. 10 migration files define RLS policies on top of it.
  PostGIS      39 migrations. Not Supabase-specific, but the `gis` schema placement is.
  pg_cron      7 migrations — matview refresh, nightly vacuum, the ingest schedule.
  pg_net       2 migrations — the cron -> Edge Function call path.
  Storage      1 bucket (`media`), upload + getPublicUrl. Small surface.
  Realtime     1 channel, broadcast-based rather than postgres_changes. Small surface.
  Edge Function  the Deno ingest worker.

THE KEY INSIGHT: the hard part is not Postgres. It is that RLS + auth.uid() + PostgREST
together ARE the application's server. Moving the database is a weekend; moving off that
trio means either reproducing it or writing a backend, and writing a backend abandons
decision 002.

That is more tractable than it sounds. auth.uid() is an ordinary SQL function reading
request.jwt.claims, which PostgREST populates from the bearer token. Mint JWTs with the
same `sub` and `role` claims, define auth.uid() ourselves, and every RLS policy keeps
working untouched. That single compatibility shim is what makes an incremental exit
possible instead of a rewrite.

OPTIONS, roughly ascending in effort

  1. Self-host the Supabase stack on Fly (postgres + PostgREST + GoTrue + Storage +
     Realtime containers). Highest fidelity — the SPA does not change at all — and the
     most operational surface to own.
  2. Fly Managed Postgres + PostgREST as a Fly app + our own JWT minting + Tigris for
     storage. Keeps RLS and the no-backend architecture; replaces GoTrue with something
     small; drops or reimplements Realtime; the ingest becomes a Fly cron machine rather
     than pg_cron -> pg_net -> Edge Function.
  3. Write a real backend API. Most freedom, abandons decision 002, largest rewrite.

Option 2 looks right if orcasite is going to Fly anyway, but the call belongs in a
decision record rather than here.

SEQUENCING THAT DE-RISKS IT
  - Nothing about this is urgent while the site works. Do it deliberately.
  - The pieces are separable and can move one at a time: storage first (smallest, and the
    ~2,700 objects want to move on maderas per CLAUDE.md, not over home internet), then
    the ingest off pg_cron/pg_net, then auth, then Postgres+PostgREST last.
  - A read-replica or logical-replication cutover keeps the map serving while the write
    path moves.
  - The DwC-A nightly build needs Postgres access from CI either way.

FIRST STEP, cheap and useful regardless: get observability we do not have today. Even on
Supabase, a way to see pg_stat_activity and connection counts would have turned this
outage from a mystery into a diagnosis.
notes:
BLOCKED pending a consolidation conversation with Orcasound (2026-08-28). Do not start.

SSO IS THE PIVOT, not a detail. The auth.uid() compatibility shim described above — mint
JWTs with matching sub/role claims, define auth.uid() ourselves, keep every RLS policy
untouched — is what makes option 2 tractable instead of a rewrite. It assumes we mint the
tokens. If identity is shared with Orcasound, that assumption is no longer ours to make,
and the answer determines which option is even available.

Also filed: precomputing the logged-out read path, which should come BEFORE any migration
rather than after. It removes PostgREST from the read side, leaving a small write API, and
would have kept the site serving through the outage that prompted this.
2026-09-27: the 'move storage objects on maderas' guidance above is withdrawn. It was a pnwmoths concern (many GB); the photo bucket is ~104 MB and the laptop is on 1 Gb fiber, so the transfer can run from anywhere.
2026-09-30: end state decided as a direction in decision 059 (docs/decisions/059-the-end-state-is-a-build-graph-with-a-small-authoritative-store.md): BeeAtlas's shape — the Stelis graph derives everything from upstream snapshots; only user-written data (~600 sightings + photos, feedback) lives in a small store on the Fly machine, expected SQLite behind a small write API. Step 3 (ingest into the build) comes first either way. Reversed to option 2 if consolidating with Orcasound means one shared Postgres; the SSO conversation still gates confirming the store.
2026-09-30 correction (Peter): salishsea will never share a database with Orcasound. The shared-Postgres reversal in the note above was an agent's extrapolation, not anything decided; decision 059 now says the Orcasound conversation decides only who issues sign-ins (how the write API verifies tokens), and 059 is accepted outright.
2026-10-05 (Peter): sign-in stays Google Sign-In for now. Step 4's write API verifies Google ID tokens itself; Orcasound-issued identity is not pursued now. Step 4 sequence proposed 2026-10-05: (1) upstream data the snapshot reads from Postgres becomes build input (register from its release, catalogue derived, Happywhale frozen file, reference tables checked in) - STARTED; (2) SQLite store + write API on Fly, replicated from day one, photos to object storage; (3) GSI verification + edit permissions in the API; (4) cutover of writes, targeted build on save; (5) retire Supabase, amend decision 002.
